9Asociación Mexicana de Vacunología, Mexico City; 10Department of Infectious Diseases, Unidad Médica de Alta Especialidad, Hospital de Gineco Pediatría 48, Instituto Mexicano del Seguro Social, León, Guanajuato; 11Research Laboratory for Infectious and Parasitic Diseases, Hospital Infantil de México Federico Gómez, Mexico City; 12Department of Pediatric Infectious Diseases, Antiguo Hospital Civil de Guadalajara Fray Antonio Alcalde, Guadalajara, Jalisco; 13Department of Infectious Diseases, Instituto Nacional de Pediatría, Mexico City; 14Department of Pediatrics, Instituto Mexicano del Seguro Social, Irapuato, Guanajuato; 15Asociación Mexicana de Infectología Pediátrica, Mexico City; 16Infectious Diseases Unit, Hospital Español, Mexico City; 17Laboratory of Inborn Errors of Metabolism, Instituto Nacional de Pediatría, Mexico City; 18Academia Mexicana de Pediatría, Mexico City, Mexico Boletín Médico del Hospital Infantil de México REVIEW ARTICLE Abstract Respiratory syncytial virus (RSV) is one of the leading causes of acute lower respiratory tract infection, bronchiolitis, pneu­ monia, and hospitalization among infants and young children, with the highest risk of severe disease observed in infants younger than six months, preterm infants, and children with bronchopulmonary dysplasia, congenital heart disease, immuno­ compromising conditions, and other underlying comorbidities. In Mexico, available evidence demonstrates a substantial cli­ nical burden and a predominant seasonal circulation from September to March. In recent years, the development of novel preventive strategies has transformed the approach to RSV prevention, particularly through maternal immunization with a bivalent prefusion F protein vaccine and passive immunoprophylaxis with long-acting monoclonal antibodies. This position statement from the Mexican Academy of Pediatrics reviews the epidemiological, clinical, and real-world effectiveness evidence regarding currently available strategies for the prevention of RSV infection in the pediatric population. Maternal vaccination between 32 and 36 weeks of gestation promotes transplacental antibody transfer and provides protection to infants during the first months of life. Monoclonal antibodies, particularly nirsevimab, have demonstrated significant reductions in lower respiratory tract infection, hospitalization, intensive care unit admission, and severe RSV-associated disease, with a favorable safety profile. This is an open access article under the CC BY-NC-ND license (http://creativecommons.org/licenses/by-nc-nd/4.0/). 212 Bol Med Hosp Infant Mex (Eng). 2026;83(4) Epidemiology of respiratory syncytial virus Respiratory syncytial virus (RSV) is an RNA virus belonging to the family Pneumoviridae and consists of 2 genotypes (A and B). RSV is specific to and patho­ genic in humans and infects cells of the respiratory tract. In 2025, RSV was the leading cause of acute lower respiratory tract infections, causing 3.6 million hospitalizations annually in children younger than 5 years and significantly increasing the risk of mortality in older adults with comorbidities. Most children infected with RSV have mild symptoms, but some develop severe disease (bronchiolitis or pneumonia). RSV is estimated to cause more than 100 000 deaths annually in children younger than 5 years, and more than 97% of these deaths occur in low- and middle-income countries.1 Recent epidemiologic data highlight the predomi­ nance of RSV-A and the high mortality burden in low- and middle-income countries, accounting for more than 95% of pediatric deaths worldwide.2 The epidemiology of RSV has attracted increasing interest in recent years, particularly in the context of the COVID-19 pandemic, which dramatically altered the transmission dynamics of various respiratory viruses. The pandemic caused by severe acute respiratory syn­ drome coronavirus 2 (SARS-CoV-2) altered seasonal RSV patterns worldwide, with a substantial decrease observed during 2020 in all countries. Atypical out­ breaks and delays in the onset of seasonal peaks were reported in several regions, suggesting accumulated susceptibility in the pediatric population. Following the pandemic, RSV showed signs of returning to prepan­ demic seasonal trends, with a more consistent recovery observed in countries in the Southern Hemisphere than in equatorial regions. The duration of RSV sea­ sonality ranged from 4 to 32 weeks across countries. El desarrollo de nuevas estrategias preventivas ha transformado el abordaje del VSR, particularmente mediante la vacunación materna con vacuna bivalente de proteína F prefusión y la inmunoprofilaxis pasiva con anticuerpos monoclonales de acción prolongada. La vacunación materna entre las 32 y 36 semanas de gestación permite la transferencia transplacentaria de anticuerpos y confiere protección al lactante durante los primeros meses de vida. Por su parte, los anticuerpos monoclonales, especialmente el nirsevimab, han demostrado reducciones significativas en infección respiratoria baja, hospitalización, ingreso a cuidados intensivos y enfermedad grave asociada a VSR, con un perfil de seguridad favorable. AMP position statement on RSV prevention SARS-CoV-2 circulation were observed in most countries, suggesting possible mechanisms of viral interference. RSV subtype A predominated in most countries after 2022.3 RSV transmission occurs primarily through direct contact and respiratory droplets, facilitating its spread in crowded settings such as schools, daycare centers, and hospitals. A systematic review and meta-analysis evaluating the burden of hospital-acquired RSV infection in children found a pooled incidence rate of 10.86 cases per 1000 person-years among hospitalized pediatric patients. The mortality rate was 11.34 deaths per 1000 person-years.4 This study highlights that hospital-acquired RSV has a case-fatality rate of 13.30%, significantly higher than that of community-acquired RSV, which usually ranges from 0% to 1.7%. Hospital-acquired RSV accounts for approximately 15.57% of all RSV hospitalizations and 22.48% of all health care-associated infections in pedi­ atric patients. This infection is a “serious and under­ recognized” cause of death; therefore, strengthening infection control and prevention strategies in hospital settings is important.4 In Latin America and the Caribbean, RSV represents a substantial disease burden. A recent meta-analysis including 156 studies from the region, mainly from Brazil (25%), Colombia (14.5%), and Argentina (13.8%), found that the highest pooled prevalence was esti­ mated among patients younger than 1 year (58%), with type A and B prevalences of 52% and 34%, respec­ tively. The incidence of RSV lower respiratory tract infection was 15 per 100 symptomatic infants younger than 2 years, with an intensive care unit (ICU) admis­ sion rate of 42%. The RSV case fatality rate was 0.6% in patients younger than 2 years, 3% in children aged 0-5 years, and 23% in high-risk patients older than 65 years.5 In Mexico, RSV is the leading cause of lower respi­ ratory tract infection and hospitalization in infants and preschool-aged children. Studies conducted at several hospitals show that RSV causes approximately 40%- 44% of hospitalizations for lower respiratory tract infec­ tion in children younger than 5 years.6,7 In a multicenter study conducted at 7 hospitals in Mexico, RSV caused 38% of pneumonia cases in children younger than 14 years during the pandemic (2021-2023) and 28% after the pandemic (2023-2025).8 At a pediatric referral hospital (2004-2008), 75% of isolated viruses were RSV; 91% of patients required hospitalization and 16% required mechanical ventilation. Among preterm infants, the RSV hospital­ ization rate during the first year of life was 9.4% in infants with bronchopulmonary dysplasia, 5.9% in those with congenital heart disease, and 2.6% in preterm infants without comorbidities.9 A recent national study (2023-2024) found severe disease (hospitalized bronchiolitis/pneumonia) in 21% of 2022 children with confirmed RSV infection.10 Risk factors Prematurity, bronchopulmonary dysplasia, and con­ genital heart disease are the main risk factors for RSV lower respiratory tract infection. RSV is more frequent and severe in infants younger than 12 months, with risk decreasing as age increases.7 Newborns aged 1-28 days and patients with comorbidities such as heart disease, immunosuppression, chronic lung disease, primary or acquired immunodeficiencies (eg, HIV), Down syn­ drome, cancer, malformations, or neurologic diseases have at least twice the risk of requiring hospitalization and a 6- to 8-fold higher risk of ICU admission.6 Seasonality RSV usually causes seasonal epidemics, with out­ breaks generally occurring between October and May in the Northern Hemisphere, between May and September in the Southern Hemisphere, and during rainy periods in tropical regions.3,4 In Mexico, epidemiologic studies reported by several authors, including studies conducted in different regions of the country, show a seasonal pattern begin­ ning in September and ending in March, including regions with tropical climates such as the Yucatán Peninsula.8,11-13 (Fig. 1). RSV is one of the most frequent pathogens causing substantial morbidity and mortality in children. These findings underscore the importance of continuous sur­ veillance, the need to optimize prevention strategies, and implementation of early diagnostic techniques to improve prevention. Several antiviral treatments are under development, and important advances have been made in vaccine research and production. An important approach is passive immunization with mono­ clonal antibodies and maternal vaccination, which have been shown to be effective in preventing severe infec­ tions in at-risk populations. Continuous epidemio­ logic surveillance of RSV, together with research and development of effective prevention strategies, is cru­ cial to addressing its public health impact. 214 Bol Med Hosp Infant Mex (Eng). 2026;83(4) Figure 1. analysis.scope_and_question: The review addresses the burden of respiratory syncytial virus (RSV) infection in Mexican infants and young children and evaluates two preventive interventions—maternal vaccination administered at 32‐36 weeks gestation and passive immunoprophylaxis with long‐acting monoclonal antibodies such as nirsevimab—within the context of Mexico’s seasonal RSV circulation.
analysis.evidence_base_and_review_method: The supplied evidence does not report the review type, searched databases, search dates, eligibility criteria, study selection process, number of included studies, or whether a meta‐analysis or formal consensus method was employed.
analysis.consensus_and_key_conclusions: The authors conclude that maternal vaccination effectively transfers antibodies to the infant and that nirsevimab markedly reduces lower respiratory tract infection, hospitalisation, ICU admission and severe RSV disease, with a favorable safety profile, indicating broad agreement on the efficacy and safety of both strategies.
analysis.controversies_and_evidence_gaps: The supplied evidence does not describe any heterogeneity, conflicting findings, methodological weaknesses, missing populations, or other specific evidence gaps related to the preventive strategies evaluated.
analysis.research_and_practice_implications: The statement recommends a complementary, progressive national strategy that incorporates maternal vaccination at 32‐36 weeks gestation and the use of nirsevimab, while emphasizing the need for ongoing surveillance of RSV seasonality, real‐world effectiveness monitoring, and assessment of implementation feasibility within the Mexican health‐care system.

analysis.summary_en: This position statement reviews RSV’s substantial disease burden among Mexican infants and outlines two preventive approaches: maternal vaccination in late pregnancy and the monoclonal antibody nirsevimab. Although methodological details of the review are not provided, the authors report consensus that both interventions are effective and safe, reducing severe disease and hospitalisation. No specific controversies or evidence gaps are identified in the supplied text. The authors propose a complementary national strategy that integrates maternal immunisation and nirsevimab use, coupled with continued surveillance of RSV seasonality and real‐world effectiveness to guide implementation in Mexico’s pediatric population.

elements_zh.consensus_and_key_conclusions: 作者得出结论,母体疫苗接种可有效将抗体转移给婴儿,而尼塞韦单抗可显著减少下呼吸道感染、住院、ICU入院和严重RSV疾病的发生,具有良好的安全性,表明对这两种策略的疗效和安全性存在广泛共识。
elements_zh.controversies_and_evidence_gaps: 所提供的证据未描述任何与所评估预防策略相关的异质性、冲突性发现、方法学缺陷、缺失人群或其他特定证据空白。
elements_zh.research_and_practice_implications: 该声明建议采用一种互补且逐步推进的国家策略,包括在妊娠32-36周期间进行母体疫苗接种和使用尼塞韦单抗,同时强调需要持续监测RSV季节性、真实世界效果以及在墨西哥医疗体系中实施的可行性。

analysis_en.scope_and_question: The review addresses the burden of respiratory syncytial virus (RSV) infection in Mexican infants and young children and evaluates two preventive interventions—maternal vaccination administered at 32‐36 weeks gestation and passive immunoprophylaxis with long‐acting monoclonal antibodies such as nirsevimab—within the context of Mexico’s seasonal RSV circulation.
analysis_en.evidence_base_and_review_method: The supplied evidence does not report the review type, searched databases, search dates, eligibility criteria, study selection process, number of included studies, or whether a meta‐analysis or formal consensus method was employed.
analysis_en.consensus_and_key_conclusions: The authors conclude that maternal vaccination effectively transfers antibodies to the infant and that nirsevimab markedly reduces lower respiratory tract infection, hospitalisation, ICU admission and severe RSV disease, with a favorable safety profile, indicating broad agreement on the efficacy and safety of both strategies.
analysis_en.controversies_and_evidence_gaps: The supplied evidence does not describe any heterogeneity, conflicting findings, methodological weaknesses, missing populations, or other specific evidence gaps related to the preventive strategies evaluated.
analysis_en.research_and_practice_implications: The statement recommends a complementary, progressive national strategy that incorporates maternal vaccination at 32‐36 weeks gestation and the use of nirsevimab, while emphasizing the need for ongoing surveillance of RSV seasonality, real‐world effectiveness monitoring, and assessment of implementation feasibility within the Mexican health‐care system.

title_zh: 墨西哥儿科学会关于预防墨西哥儿童群体呼吸道合胞病毒(RSV)感染策略的立场声明
source_body_en: Respiratory syncytial virus (RSV) is one of the leading causes of acute lower respiratory tract infection, bronchiolitis, pneumonia, and hospitalization among infants and young children, with the highest risk of severe disease observed in infants younger than six months, preterm infants, and children with bronchopulmonary dysplasia, congenital heart disease, immunocompromising conditions, and other underlying comorbidities.In Mexico, available evidence demonstrates a substantial clinical burden and a predominant seasonal circulation from September to March.In recent years, the development of novel preventive strategies has transformed the approach to RSV prevention, particularly through maternal immunization with a bivalent prefusion F protein vaccine and passive immunoprophylaxis with long-acting monoclonal antibodies.This position statement from the Mexican Academy of Pediatrics reviews the epidemiological, clinical, and real-world effectiveness evidence regarding currently available strategies for the prevention of RSV infection in the pediatric population.Maternal vaccination between 32 and 36 weeks of gestation promotes transplacental antibody transfer and provides protection to infants during the first months of life.Monoclonal antibodies, particularly nirsevimab, have demonstrated significant reductions in lower respiratory tract infection, hospitalization, intensive care unit admission, and severe RSV-associated disease, with a favorable safety profile.Based on disease burden, national seasonality, availability of preventive products, and the characteristics of the Mexican health care system, the Mexican Academy of Pediatrics proposes a complementary and progressive strategy
abstract_zh: 呼吸道合胞病毒(RSV)是导致婴幼儿和儿童急性下呼吸道感染、毛细支气管炎、肺炎和住院的主要原因之一,其中6个月以下婴儿、早产儿以及患有支气管肺发育不良、先天性心脏病、免疫抑制状况及其他基础合并症的儿童面临最严重的疾病风险。在墨西哥,现有证据表明RSV感染具有显著的临床负担,并且主要在9月至3月期间呈现季节性流行。近年来,新型预防策略的发展改变了RSV预防的方法,特别是在通过双价前融合F蛋白疫苗进行母体免疫接种以及使用长效单克隆抗体进行被动免疫预防方面。墨西哥儿科学会发布的这一立场声明回顾了目前针对儿童群体RSV感染预防策略的流行病学、临床和真实世界效果证据。在妊娠32至36周期间进行的母体疫苗接种可促进抗体通过胎盘转移,并在婴儿出生后的最初几个月内提供保护。单克隆抗体,特别是尼塞韦单抗,已被证明可显著降低下呼吸道感染、住院、重症监护病房入院以及严重RSV相关疾病的发病率,且具有良好的安全性。基于疾病负担、国家季节性特征、预防产品的可获得性以及墨西哥医疗体系的特性,墨西哥儿科学会建议采用一种互补且逐步推进的国家策略。

title: Pediatric RSV-associated lower respiratory tract infection burden in G20 countries in 2023
abstract: Respiratory syncytial virus (RSV) is a leading cause of childhood lower respiratory infections, but updated G20 burden estimates are lacking. Using the Global Burden of Disease 2023 database, we analyzed deaths and disability-adjusted life years (DALYs) for RSV-associated lower respiratory infections in children aged 0–14 years across G20 members from 1990 to 2023, with stratification by sex, age, and country. In 2023, an estimated 5,373 deaths and 483,162 DALYs occurred, with mortality and DALY rates having declined by ∼5.5% annually since 1990. The COVID-19 pandemic drove burden to a historic low in 2021, but a marked rebound followed in 2022–2023, though rates remained below pre-pandemic levels. Infants aged <1 year bore the heaviest burden (mortality 8.688 per 100,000), and India ranked highest, whereas Australia ranked lowest. Burden strongly correlated inversely with Sociodemographic Index. These findings highlight the need for precision prevention, targeting the youngest children and lower-resource G20 members.

Using the Global Burden of Disease 2023 database, we analyzed deaths and disability-adjusted life years (DALYs) for RSV-associated lower respiratory infections in children aged 0–14 years across G20 members from 1990 to 2023, with stratification by sex, age, and country. In 2023, an estimated 5,373 deaths and 483,162 DALYs occurred, with mortality and DALY rates having declined by ∼5.5% annually since 1990. The COVID-19 pandemic drove burden to a historic low in 2021, but a marked rebound followed in 2022–2023, though rates remained below pre-pandemic levels. Infants aged <1 year bore the heaviest burden (mortality 8.688 per 100,000), and India ranked highest, whereas Australia ranked lowest. Burden strongly correlated inversely with Sociodemographic Index. These findings highlight the need for precision prevention, targeting the youngest children and lower-resource G20 members.

full_text: ABSTRACTHerpes zoster (HZ) causes substantial morbidity, yet global uptake remains suboptimal where the vaccine is excluded from universal coverage. Taiwan exemplifies such a self-payment setting, with the HZ vaccine self-financed and local government subsidies restricted to limited eligible groups. This study analyzed data from a nationwide, web-based cross-sectional survey of adults aged ≥18y fielded in 2025, examining factors associated with HZ vaccination behavior, intention, and willingness to pay (WTP). Of 1690 respondents, 281 (16.6%) were vaccinated; among 1409 unvaccinated, 1140 (80.9%) were willing to vaccinate. Factors associated with HZ vaccination included age ≥65y (OR: 1.59; 95% CI: 1.12–2.25), prior HZ infection (OR: 1.62; 1.23–2.15), prior receipt of influenza, pneumococcal, or respiratory syncytial virus (RSV) vaccines (OR: 3.32; 2.26–4.89), and awareness of local subsidy programs (OR: 2.30; 1.70–3.12). Among unvaccinated respondents, intention was most strongly associated with high concern about HZ (OR: 3.62; 2.67–4.90). When each prior vaccine was examined separately, prior receipt of self-paid RSV (OR: 5.35; 3.44–8.31) and pneumococcal vaccines (OR: 3.48; 2.54–4.75) showed stronger associations with HZ vaccination than coronavirus disease 2019 (OR: 1.50; 1.04–2.16) or influenza vaccines (OR: 1.51; 1.13–2.02). The median WTP rose stepwise across vaccination statuses (unvaccinated-unwilling: USD 8.2, unvaccinated-willing: USD 32.8, vaccinated: USD 65.6; p < .001), yet all values remained below the market price. In this self-payment setting, HZ vaccination was constrained by affordability rather than lack of motivation. Expanding coverage will require policy action on cost, while prior receipt of self-paid adult vaccines offers a clinically identifiable marker for targeted counseling. MethodsStudy design and respondentsThis study is an analysis of a dataset from the 2025 National Survey on Herpes Zoster Knowledge and Vaccination Attitudes, a nationwide survey commissioned by the Taiwan Association of Family Medicine as a public-opinion poll. The survey was conducted from August 20 to September 2, 2025, by an independent professional survey research organization among adults aged 18 y and older. Participants were recruited through active digital distribution across various online platforms, including e-mails, websites, social media, and search engines. To ensure a representative sample, stratified random sampling was performed based on sex, age, and residential area. This recruitment methodology was widely validated and utilized in recent large-scale epidemiological web surveys.24,25 To prevent duplicate responses and ensure the uniqueness of each participant, digital behavioral profiling and user tagging techniques were integrated into the data collection process. Self-reported demographic information was cross-verified using digital behavioral data matching to ensure data accuracy and reliability.26 Participation in the parent survey was voluntary; respondents were informed of its purpose and agreed to participate before answering the questionnaire, and the survey collected no personally identifiable information. The present analysis of this existing dataset was approved by the Institutional Review Board of National Cheng Kung University Hospital before any analysis was undertaken, with a waiver of informed consent (No. B-ER-115–034, April 2, 2026). This study was conducted in accordance with the principles of the Declaration of Helsinki.Questionnaire surveyThe survey instrument was developed for the parent survey by an expert panel convened by the Taiwan Association of Family Medicine. It was adapted from two previously published studies27,28 and further refined through expert consensus. Each item was reviewed for relevance, accuracy, and clarity by a multidisciplinary panel of specialists in family medicine, geriatrics, and preventive medicine. The panel review established content validity and confirmed cultural and linguistic appropriateness for the Taiwanese setting. Because the instrument used single-item behavioral, attitudinal, and economic measures rather than multi-item latent-construct scales, content validity rather than internal consistency was the appropriate validation standard. The final instrument consisted of 15 items in five sections: (1) demographics and medical history; (2) disease knowledge and risk perception; (3) HZ vaccination behavior, intention, and barriers; (4) prior adult vaccination history; and (5) awareness of local subsidy programs and WTP. Items were presented in true/false, multiple-choice, and 10-point numeric rating scale formats. The questionnaire was developed in Chinese. Demographics and medical history: This section recorded respondents’ sex, age, and residential area (covering 22 administrative divisions in Taiwan). Clinical health status was assessed based on 10 chronic conditions, including diabetes, hypertension, cardiovascular diseases, stroke, chronic respiratory diseases, chronic kidney disease, liver cirrhosis, malignancy, other immunocompromising conditions, and the use of immunosuppressive therapies. These conditions were combined into a single composite indicator owing to sparse individual categories. Personal history of HZ was also documented.Disease knowledge and risk perception: Knowledge of HZ was assessed based on four key clinical facts: high lifetime incidence, high-risk populations, potential for recurrence, and its association with a history of chickenpox. Respondents used 1–10 point scales to rate the perceived pain severity of HZ (1: not painful to 10: most severe pain), its perceived impact on daily life (1: no impact to 10: total disruption), and their level of concern about HZ (1: not concerned to 10: extremely concerned). Because only a minority of respondents had personally experienced HZ, these items were framed as perceptions: respondents with a prior episode answered from personal experience, and those without answered on the basis of their existing knowledge or impression of the disease.HZ vaccination behavior, intention, and barriers: HZ vaccination status was assessed for all individuals. Unvaccinated individuals were further queried regarding their future intention to receive the vaccine. Accordingly, respondents were categorized as (1) vaccinated individuals, (2) unvaccinated individuals willing to be vaccinated (“unvaccinated-willing”), and (3) unvaccinated individuals unwilling to be vaccinated (“unvaccinated-unwilling”). From a list of 10 predefined barriers, unvaccinated participants identified their reasons for not being vaccinated, with multiple selections permitted.Prior adult vaccination history: A history of other adult vaccinations was collected for four vaccines: COVID-19, influenza, pneumococcal, and RSV. These vaccines differ in their funding status in Taiwan. COVID-19 vaccines have been publicly funded for all adults, and influenza vaccines have been publicly funded for adults aged ≥50 y and other priority groups (e.g., healthcare workers, patients with chronic medical illness). The pneumococcal vaccine was self-financed for most adults until October 2023, when public funding was extended to adults aged ≥65 y and high-risk groups. The RSV vaccine, introduced in Taiwan in 2024, has remained entirely self-paid.Awareness of local subsidy programs and willingness to pay: Respondents were asked about their awareness of the localized and conditional HZ vaccine subsidy programs offered by selected local governments in Taiwan. WTP was assessed via an open-ended question, in which participants reported the maximum amount they were willing to pay out-of-pocket for the HZ vaccine. Values were collected in New Taiwan Dollars (TWD) and converted to US Dollars (USD) using the average exchange rate during the survey period (30.5 TWD = 1 USD).Statistical analysisDescriptive statistics are presented as counts and percentages. Comparisons across groups were conducted using χ2 tests. Clinical health status was dichotomized based on the diagnosis of at least one of 10 chronic conditions. Perception scales (pain severity, impact on daily life, and concern level) were rated on 1–10 numeric rating scales and dichotomized into low (1–6) and high (7–10) groups, consistent with the commonly used cutoff of ≥7 to denote a high level on numeric rating scales.Multivariable logistic regression models were employed to identify independent factors associated with two primary outcomes: (1) HZ vaccination behavior (vaccinated vs. unvaccinated) among the total population, and (2) HZ vaccination intention (willing vs. unwilling) among unvaccinated individuals. These models were adjusted for sex, age, chronic medical illness, history of HZ, concern level regarding HZ, and awareness of local subsidy programs. Six logistic regression models were constructed for each primary outcome, each containing a different prior vaccination variable. This approach evaluated the influence of prior immunization at multiple levels while avoiding multicollinearity. Models 1 to 4 examined the influence of each individual prior vaccine separately, with prior receipt of COVID-19 vaccine (Model 1), influenza vaccine (Model 2), pneumococcal vaccine (Model 3), and RSV vaccine (Model 4) as the predictors of interest. Models 5 and 6 used composite measures. Model 5 served as the primary composite analysis, examining prior receipt of any non-COVID-19 adult vaccine (influenza, pneumococcal, or RSV); this composite was designed to isolate the influence of vaccinations requiring more active health-seeking behavior, given that the near-universal COVID-19 vaccination coverage in Taiwan would otherwise obscure such associations. Model 6 was conducted as a sensitivity analysis, examining prior receipt of any adult vaccine (COVID-19, influenza, pneumococcal, or RSV), to assess whether the composite findings remained robust when the universally funded COVID-19 vaccine was included. As a further sensitivity analysis, the primary multivariable models were repeated with the sample restricted to respondents aged ≥50 y, the principal target age for HZ vaccination.For the WTP analysis, cumulative distribution curves were generated to visualize the maximum out-of-pocket amounts participants were willing to pay, an approach adopted from previous vaccine WTP studies.29,30 For comparisons among three groups stratified by HZ vaccination behavior and intention (vaccinated, unvaccinated-willing, and unvaccinated-unwilling), the Kruskal‒Wallis test was used, followed by Dunn’s post-hoc test with Bonferroni correction for pairwise comparisons. For comparisons between two groups stratified by history of other non-COVID-19 adult vaccinations (yes vs. no), the Mann‒Whitney U test was used. Effect sizes were reported as eta-squared (η2) for Kruskal‒Wallis and r (|Z|/√N) for Mann‒Whitney U tests.All analyses were performed using IBM SPSS Statistics (version 27.0; IBM Corp., Armonk, NY, USA). A p value less than .05 was considered statistically significant. The survey was conducted from August 20 to September 2, 2025, by an independent professional survey research organization among adults aged 18 y and older. This recruitment methodology was widely validated and utilized in recent large-scale epidemiological web surveys.24,25 To prevent duplicate responses and ensure the uniqueness of each participant, digital behavioral profiling and user tagging techniques were integrated into the data collection process. Self-reported demographic information was cross-verified using digital behavioral data matching to ensure data accuracy and reliability.26 Participation in the parent survey was voluntary; respondents were informed of its purpose and agreed to participate before answering the questionnaire, and the survey collected no personally identifiable information. The present analysis of this existing dataset was approved by the Institutional Review Board of National Cheng Kung University Hospital before any analysis was undertaken, with a waiver of informed consent (No. B-ER-115–034, April 2, 2026). This study was conducted in accordance with the principles of the Declaration of Helsinki. full_text_sections.discussion: DiscussionIn this nationwide cross-sectional survey of adults examining HZ vaccination behavior and intention in a predominantly self-payment setting, four principal findings emerged. First, vaccination intention substantially exceeded actual uptake, indicating a pronounced intention–behavior gap. Second, the correlates of intention and behavior diverged: concern about HZ was associated with intention only, and a prior HZ episode with behavior only. Third, prior receipt of self-paid adult vaccines showed the strongest association with vaccination behavior. Fourth, the public’s WTP fell well below the market price of HZ vaccine and was lowest among individuals with lower vaccine acceptance. Together, these findings indicate that intention and behavior are associated with distinct factors, a pattern consistent with motivational factors relating to intention and economic factors relating to uptake.In this self-payment setting, HZ vaccination coverage and intention were comparable to or higher than most international reports, yet this favorable engagement did not translate proportionally into actual uptake. The HZ vaccination coverage in this study was 21.0% among adults aged ≥50 y and 26.2% among those aged ≥65 y. This exceeds the coverage rates reported in China (0.79% among those aged ≥40 y in 2024)16 and the United States (17% among those aged ≥50 y in 2021)13 but remains lower than in Australia (32% among those aged ≥65 y in 2019–2020).15 Notably, four in five unvaccinated respondents (1140 of 1409, 80.9%) were willing to vaccinate, substantially exceeding the 55.74% pooled global willingness rate reported in a 2023 systematic review and meta-analysis.31 The contrast between this strong vaccination intention and the suboptimal actual coverage indicates that public attitude is unlikely to be the primary obstacle. Rather, a substantive intention–behavior gap separates the willing from the vaccinated.Concern level regarding HZ was the factor most strongly associated with vaccination intention but was not associated with actual behavior. Among the unvaccinated respondents, those with high concern levels had more than three times the odds of expressing willingness to vaccinate (OR: 3.62; 95% CI: 2.67–4.90). However, concern level was not independently associated with actual HZ vaccination. This discrepancy suggests that while concern accompanies the intention to be immunized, concern alone appears insufficient to translate intention into actual vaccination under self-payment conditions. Whereas multiple cross-sectional studies have demonstrated that higher perceived risk is associated with greater willingness to receive the HZ vaccine,32–35 our analysis extends these findings by showing that this motivational pathway does not appear to translate into actual uptake when cost remains a barrier.Conversely, a prior HZ infection was associated with actual vaccination but not with future intention among unvaccinated individuals. Stated differently, among those who had experienced HZ but remained unvaccinated, prior infection was not associated with willingness to vaccinate. This null association can be explained by the pattern of self-reported reasons for non-vaccination shown in Figure 1. Among unvaccinated respondents, “perceived lack of need due to prior HZ history” was cited as a barrier more than three times as often by the unwilling group than the willing group (18.6% vs. 5.9%, p < .001; Figure 1). This suggests that a substantial proportion of people with prior HZ believe a single episode confers lasting protection and therefore see no reason to vaccinate. This belief, however, overlooks the well-documented potential for HZ recurrence, and current Advisory Committee on Immunization Practices (ACIP) guidelines explicitly recommend HZ vaccination irrespective of prior HZ history.9,36,37 Public education should be targeted rather than generic. Adults with a prior HZ episode are identifiable in routine practice and remain at risk of recurrence, and counseling at diagnosis or subsequent visits could address recurrence risk, post-episode vaccine efficacy, and the related misconceptions of low susceptibility and severity.Whereas prior HZ history reflects direct disease experience, prior receipt of other adult vaccinations represents a different behavioral pathway – one that emerged as an even stronger predictor of HZ vaccination uptake. A history of other non-COVID-19 adult vaccinations was the strongest predictor of HZ vaccination behavior and an independent predictor of intention. The vaccine-specific findings revealed a clear gradient by funding mechanism of each prior vaccine. The entirely self-paid RSV vaccine showed the strongest association (Model 4, OR: 5.35), followed by the recently transitioned pneumococcal vaccine (Model 3, OR: 3.48), and then the long-publicly-funded influenza and COVID-19 vaccines (Models 2 and 1: OR: 1.51 and 1.50, respectively). This gradient suggests that the association reflects individuals’ out-of-pocket spending on preventive care rather than vaccination habits per se. To our knowledge, this is the first study to demonstrate a funding-mechanism gradient in prior vaccination as a predictor of HZ vaccine uptake, providing a novel framework for understanding vaccination decisions in self-payment settings.Clinical risk groups warrant separate consideration. Diabetes is associated with an approximately 40% increase in HZ incidence.38,39 Immunocompromising conditions and immunosuppressive therapies raise the risk of HZ, postherpetic neuralgia, disseminated disease, and HZ-related hospitalization.40 ACIP therefore recommends RZV for immunodeficient or immunosuppressed adults from age 19.9 Nonetheless, chronic medical illness was not associated with vaccination behavior or intention. This null association persisted across all six regression models (Tables 2 and 3) and in the analysis restricted to adults aged ≥50 y (Supplementary Table 1). Elevated clinical risk therefore did not distinguish those who vaccinated from those who did not. This finding should be interpreted with caution. Individual conditions were too sparse for stable estimation and were analyzed as a single composite indicator. This indicator grouped severely immunosuppressed patients with those having more common conditions, and such aggregation may have diluted a genuine association among the most immunocompromised. Even so, the absence of any signal suggests that clinical risk is not currently a principal driver of vaccination in this self-payment setting. Clinician-initiated counseling could address this gap.Across these findings, affordability emerged as the central obstacle separating intention from behavior, and our data build a cumulative case for this conclusion through two lines of evidence. First, cost was the most frequently cited barrier in both unvaccinated subgroups and was cited more often by the willing group than by the unwilling group (62.1% vs. 40.9%, p < .001; Figure 1). This pattern is consistent with prior literature identifying high vaccine cost as the primary barrier to HZ vaccination28,33,41,42 and indicates that cost is the proximal obstacle particularly for those who would otherwise vaccinate. Second, our WTP analysis provides direct quantitative evidence that financial constraints are not merely perceived but objectively present, and that this constraint scales with vaccine acceptance. Figure 2(A) reveals a stepwise WTP gradient across groups defined by HZ vaccination behavior and intention (vaccinated USD 65.6 > unvaccinated-willing USD 32.8 > unvaccinated-unwilling USD 8.2; all pairwise p < .001). Figure 2(B) also shows a parallel pattern when respondents were stratified by history of other non-COVID-19 adult vaccinations (with vs. without history: USD 32.8 vs. USD 16.4, p < .001). Together, these analyses demonstrate that individuals with lower vaccine acceptance – whether defined by HZ behavior and intention or by prior adult vacci…
full_text_sections.conclusion: ConclusionIn this self-payment setting, lower HZ vaccination uptake was associated more with cost barriers than with a lack of motivation. Measured WTP fell substantially below the market price of RZV. Concern about HZ was associated with vaccination intention; however, this association alone did not appear sufficient to close the intention–behavior gap. These findings suggest that expanding coverage will likely require policy action on cost. In parallel, prior receipt of self-paid adult vaccines may offer a clinically identifiable marker for targeting counseling and co-administration efforts.
full_text_sections.other: IntroductionHerpes zoster (HZ), the clinical reactivation of latent varicella-zoster virus, affects approximately one in three persons during their lifetime, with the highest burden among older adults.1–4 Acute herpetic neuralgia and postherpetic neuralgia (PHN) – the most common long-term complication – substantially impair quality of life and functional independence.5 Beyond the established age-related risk, recent evidence indicates that prior coronavirus disease 2019 (COVID-19) infection further increases the one-year risk of HZ (hazard ratios, 1.59 to 2.16), broadening the population at risk.6,7Two efficacious vaccines are available for primary prevention. The live attenuated zoster vaccine reduces the incidence of HZ and PHN by 67% and 83% in the first year following administration.8 The recombinant zoster vaccine (RZV), now the preferred option in most national programs,9 reduces the risk of HZ and PHN by 97.2% and 91.2%, respectively, with a complete two-dose regimen.10 Despite this efficacy, global uptake remains suboptimal,11–13 in part because HZ vaccination is excluded from universal national health coverage in many countries and remains primarily an out-of-pocket expense.14 Uptake varies markedly by funding mechanism. Coverage reaches approximately one-third of eligible older adults where HZ vaccination is publicly funded and nationally recommended (32% among adults aged ≥65 y in Australia15), but is substantially lower where the vaccine remains an out-of-pocket expense (0.79% among adults aged ≥40 y in China16). This contrast underscores the value of examining the determinants of uptake specifically under self-payment conditions, where the decision to vaccinate is also a decision to pay.Taiwan provides an instructive case of such a self-payment setting, where the HZ vaccine is predominantly funded out-of-pocket rather than through universal coverage. The HZ vaccine is not included in Taiwan’s National Health Insurance program or the national immunization schedule. Although some local governments offer partial subsidies, eligibility is mostly restricted to economically disadvantaged individuals, leaving most adults to pay the full cost out-of-pocket. Understanding what drives vaccination uptake under such self-payment conditions is therefore relevant not only to Taiwan but also to the many regions where comprehensive public funding has yet to be established. Behavioral theory anticipates that motivation alone may not suffice in such settings. Both the Health Belief Model and the 5C framework of vaccination psychology treat cost as a structural barrier capable of overriding favorable attitudes,17–20 and the resulting intention–behavior gap is well documented across health behaviors.21 We therefore analyzed vaccination intention and behavior as separate outcomes.Two questions central to expanding HZ vaccination coverage in a self-payment setting remain inadequately addressed. First, it is unclear whether adults who have received other vaccines are more likely to receive the HZ vaccine. Prior vaccination behavior may reflect general health-seeking tendencies, vaccine confidence, or regular healthcare contact, which can predict future vaccination decisions.22,23 It is also unknown whether this association differs depending on whether the prior vaccine was publicly funded or paid out-of-pocket. Adults who have already paid out-of-pocket for one vaccine may be more willing to do so for additional self-paid vaccines such as HZ, but this hypothesis has not been tested. Second, the determinants of willingness to pay (WTP) for the HZ vaccine remain poorly understood, particularly whether WTP is influenced by vaccination behavior, intention, and prior adult vaccination history.To address these gaps and to provide insights applicable to similar self-payment settings worldwide, we analyzed data from a nationwide, web-based cross-sectional survey of adults in Taiwan, with the aim of identifying what separates the intention to vaccinate from the act of vaccinating when the cost is borne by the individual. Specifically, we aimed to (1) determine the prevalence of HZ vaccination and the intention to vaccinate among unvaccinated adults; (2) identify factors independently associated with vaccination behavior and intention, with particular focus on the influence of prior adult vaccination history; and (3) assess WTP for the HZ vaccine, including its variation by vaccination behavior, intention, and prior adult vaccination history. Questionnaire surveyThe survey instrument was developed for the parent survey by an expert panel convened by the Taiwan Association of Family Medicine. It was adapted from two previously published studies27,28 and further refined through expert consensus. Each item was reviewed for relevance, accuracy, and clarity by a multidisciplinary panel of specialists in family medicine, geriatrics, and preventive medicine. The panel review established content validity and confirmed cultural and linguistic appropriateness for the Taiwanese setting. Because the instrument used single-item behavioral, attitudinal, and economic measures rather than multi-item latent-construct scales, content validity rather than internal consistency was the appropriate validation standard. The final instrument consisted of 15 items in five sections: (1) demographics and medical history; (2) disease knowledge and risk perception; (3) HZ vaccination behavior, intention, and barriers; (4) prior adult vaccination history; and (5) awareness of local subsidy programs and WTP. Items were presented in true/false, multiple-choice, and 10-point numeric rating scale formats. The questionnaire was developed in Chinese. Demographics and medical history: This section recorded respondents’ sex, age, and residential area (covering 22 administrative divisions in Taiwan). Clinical health status was assessed based on 10 chronic conditions, including diabetes, hypertension, cardiovascular diseases, stroke, chronic respiratory diseases, chronic kidney disease, liver cirrhosis, malignancy, other immunocompromising conditions, and the use of immunosuppressive therapies. These conditions were combined into a single composite indicator owing to sparse individual categories. Personal history of HZ was also documented.Disease knowledge and risk perception: Knowledge of HZ was assessed based on four key clinical facts: high lifetime incidence, high-risk populations, potential for recurrence, and its association with a history of chickenpox. Respondents used 1–10 point scales to rate the perceived pain severity of HZ (1: not painful to 10: most severe pain), its perceived impact on daily life (1: no impact to 10: total disruption), and their level of concern about HZ (1: not concerned to 10: extremely concerned). Because only a minority of respondents had personally experienced HZ, these items were framed as perceptions: respondents with a prior episode answered from personal experience, and those without answered on the basis of their existing knowledge or impression of the disease.HZ vaccination behavior, intention, and barriers: HZ vaccination status was assessed for all individuals. Unvaccinated individuals were further queried regarding their future intention to receive the vaccine. Accordingly, respondents were categorized as (1) vaccinated individuals, (2) unvaccinated individuals willing to be vaccinated (“unvaccinated-willing”), and (3) unvaccinated individuals unwilling to be vaccinated (“unvaccinated-unwilling”). From a list of 10 predefined barriers, unvaccinated participants identified their reasons for not being vaccinated, with multiple selections permitted.Prior adult vaccination history: A history of other adult vaccinations was collected for four vaccines: COVID-19, influenza, pneumococcal, and RSV. analysis.research_question_and_background: This study aimed to understand factors influencing herpes zoster (HZ) vaccination behavior and intention in a self-payment setting, addressing the gap in knowledge about how affordability and motivation interact in vaccine uptake.
analysis.study_design_and_population: A nationwide, web-based cross-sectional survey of adults aged ≥18 years was conducted in 2025, with participants recruited through active digital distribution across online platforms. The sample included 1690 respondents categorized into three groups based on their HZ vaccination status.
analysis.methods: Clinical health status was assessed based on 10 chronic conditions, and perceived pain severity, impact on daily life, and concern levels were self-rated on 1–10 numeric scales. Logistic regression models were used to analyze associations between prior vaccination history and HZ vaccination behavior or intention, with six separate models constructed for each outcome.
analysis.main_results: HZ vaccination behavior was significantly associated with age ≥65 years (OR: 1.59; 95% CI: 1.12–2.25), prior HZ infection (OR: 1.62; 95% CI: 1.23–2.15), prior receipt of non-COVID-19 adult vaccines (OR: 3.32; 95% CI: 2.26–4.89), and awareness of local subsidy programs (OR: 2.30; 95% CI: 1.70–3.12).
analysis.interpretation_and_novelty: The study highlights that prior receipt of non-COVID-19 adult vaccines, particularly RSV and pneumococcal vaccines, is strongly associated with HZ vaccination behavior, suggesting a potential link between health-seeking behaviors and vaccine uptake.
analysis.scientific_and_public_health_significanc: These findings can inform public health strategies to improve HZ vaccination rates by leveraging existing vaccination behaviors and promoting awareness of subsidy programs to reduce financial barriers.
analysis.limitations_and_evidence_strength: The study is limited by its reliance on self-reported data and the potential for recall bias. However, the use of logistic regression models and sensitivity analyses strengthens the evidence, supporting a moderate confidence assessment.

analysis.summary_en: This study investigated factors influencing herpes zoster (HZ) vaccination behavior and intention in a self-payment setting, focusing on a nationwide survey of 1690 adults. It found that age ≥65 years, prior HZ infection, and prior receipt of non-COVID-19 adult vaccines were significantly associated with HZ vaccination behavior. The study also noted that awareness of local subsidy programs increased the likelihood of vaccination. The median willingness to pay for the HZ vaccine was below the market price, indicating affordability as a barrier. The research highlights the importance of health-seeking behaviors and financial incentives in vaccine uptake, with implications for improving public health strategies. While the study has limitations due to self-reporting, the use of logistic regression models and sensitivity analyses provides moderate confidence in the findings.

elements_en.main_results: HZ vaccination behavior was significantly associated with age ≥65 years (OR: 1.59; 95% CI: 1.12–2.25), prior HZ infection (OR: 1.62; 95% CI: 1.23–2.15), prior receipt of non-COVID-19 adult vaccines (OR: 3.32; 95% CI: 2.26–4.89), and awareness of local subsidy programs (OR: 2.30; 95% CI: 1.70–3.12).
elements_en.interpretation_and_novelty: The study highlights that prior receipt of non-COVID-19 adult vaccines, particularly RSV and pneumococcal vaccines, is strongly associated with HZ vaccination behavior, suggesting a potential link between health-seeking behaviors and vaccine uptake.
elements_en.scientific_and_public_health_significanc: These findings can inform public health strategies to improve HZ vaccination rates by leveraging existing vaccination behaviors and promoting awareness of subsidy programs to reduce financial barriers.
elements_en.limitations_and_evidence_strength: The study is limited by its reliance on self-reported data and the potential for recall bias. However, the use of logistic regression models and sensitivity analyses strengthens the evidence, supporting a moderate confidence assessment.

elements_zh.study_design_and_population: 2025年进行了一项全国范围的网络横断面调查,调查对象为≥18岁的成年人,通过在线平台的主动数字分发招募参与者。样本包括1690名受访者,根据其HZ 疫苗接种状态分为三组。

elements_zh.main_results: HZ 疫苗接种行为与年龄≥65岁(OR:1.59;95% CI:1.12–2.25)、既往HZ感染史(OR:1.62;95% CI:1.23–2.15)、既往接受过非新冠19成人疫苗史(OR:3.32;95% CI:2.26–4.89)以及知晓本地补贴计划(OR:2.30;95% CI:1.70–3.12)显著相关。
elements_zh.interpretation_and_novelty: 本研究强调,既往接受过非新冠19成人疫苗,特别是呼吸道合胞病毒(RSV)和肺炎球菌疫苗,与HZ 疫苗接种行为有显著关联,这表明健康行为寻求与疫苗接种之间可能存在潜在联系。

source_body_en: This study analyzed data from a nationwide, web-based cross-sectional survey of adults aged ≥18y fielded in 2025, examining factors associated with HZ vaccination behavior, intention, and willingness to pay (WTP). MethodsStudy design and respondentsThis study is an analysis of a dataset from the 2025 National Survey on Herpes Zoster Knowledge and Vaccination Attitudes, a nationwide survey commissioned by the Taiwan Association of Family Medicine as a public-opinion poll. The present analysis of this existing dataset was approved by the Institutional Review Board of National Cheng Kung University Hospital before any analysis was undertaken, with a waiver of informed consent (No. This study was conducted in accordance with the principles of the Declaration of Helsinki.Questionnaire surveyThe survey instrument was developed for the parent survey by an expert panel convened by the Taiwan Association of Family Medicine. The panel review established content validity and confirmed cultural and linguistic appropriateness for the Taiwanese setting. Perceived pain severity, perceived impact on daily life, and concern levels were self-rated on a scale of 1–10, based on respondents’ personal experience or their existing knowledge or impression of the disease.Factors associated with herpes zoster vaccination behavior and vaccination intentionMultivariable logistic regression analysis demonstrated that HZ vaccination behavior was significantly associated with age ≥65 y (odds ratio [OR]: 1.59, 95% confidence interval [CI]: 1.12–2.25), a history of HZ (OR: 1.62, 95% CI: 1.23–2.15), a history of other non-COVID-19 adult vaccinations (OR: 3.32, 95% CI: 2.26–4.89), and awareness of local subsidy programs (OR: 2.30, 95% CI: 1.70–3.12) (Table 2). full_text: Transcriptional heterogeneity drives malignant progression, yet how it emerges within tumors remains unclear. By combining genetic perturbation and lineage tracing with parallel single-cell multiomics, we tracked the consequences of ARID1A loss within individual clonal lineages. ARID1A deficiency increased transcriptional variability both within and across clones, recurrently giving rise to diverse transcriptional profiles that did not converge on a common, coordinated pattern. This variability was accompanied by broadened chromatin accessibility at normally silenced loci and depended on residual SMARCA4 activity. Clones in which this variability was prominent showed no growth advantage under standard conditions but were preferentially recovered under specific environmental stresses and during lung colonization, a context dependence consistent with bet-hedging. Our findings suggest that loss of an epigenetic regulator can promote tumor evolution by relaxing transcriptional constraints and widening the range of phenotypes accessible to a clonal lineage, rather than by imposing a single fixed phenotype. MATERIALS AND METHODSCell culture and reagentsBxPC3, HPAC, and SUIT-2 cells were cultured in RPMI 1640 medium (Nacalai Tesque) supplemented with 10% fetal bovine serum (FBS) and penicillin/streptomycin (Sigma-Aldrich) in a 5% CO2 incubator at 37°C. SW1990 cells were cultured in Dulbecco’s modified Eagle’s medium supplemented with 10% FBS and penicillin/streptomycin. HPAFII cells were cultured in minimum essential medium (MEM) with Earle’s Salts medium (Nacalai Tesque) supplemented with 10% FBS, sodium pyruvate, and penicillin/streptomycin (Sigma-Aldrich) in a 5% CO2 incubator at 37°C. All cell lines tested negative for Mycoplasma. Some BxPC3 clones were incubated with 1 μM AU-15330 (Selleck) or dimethyl sulfoxide (DMSO) (Sigma-Aldrich) for 24 hours (Western blot and scRNA-seq) or 4 hours (scATAC-seq).Cell proliferationTo measure cell proliferation, BxPC3 clonal populations were seeded in 96-well plates at a density of 3125 cells/cm2. The cells were cultured for 7 days, during which phase-contrast images were acquired every 24 hours using a 4× objective on an IncuCyte SX5 Live-Cell Analysis System (Sartorius). Furthermore, confluence was automatically quantified at each time point using the integrated IncuCyte analysis software.Morphological classification of the clonal populationsTo assess the morphological heterogeneity among the clonal populations, bright-field images were captured for each clone using a BZ-X700 microscope (Keyence). The clones were classified into six predefined morphological types (Types 1–6) based on a stepwise decision-making process.First, if the average cell diameter was ≥20 μm, then the clone was assigned to type 6. If this criterion was not met, then colony-level features were assessed. Clones, in which cells formed tightly packed and condensed colonies, were categorized as type 2. Clones with looser intercellular contacts and scattered arrangements, which were suggestive of a mesenchymal-like morphology, were classified as type 5. If the cells appeared flattened, with an enlarged surface area, prominent perinuclear halos, or surface wrinkling, then the clone was assigned to type 4. Clones containing cells with an average diameter exceeding 11 μm—larger than that of the parental line—were designated as type 3. Clones that did not meet these criteria and resembled the morphology of the parental cell line, characterized by cohesive growth and an epithelial-like appearance, were categorized as type 1.Reverse transcription quantitative polymerase chain reactionTotal RNA was extracted using the RNeasy Plus Mini Kit (QIAGEN) according to the manufacturer’s instructions. Reverse transcription was done using the PrimeScript RT Master Mix (TaKaRa). Quantitative PCR was carried out on a StepOnePlus Real-Time PCR System (Thermo Fisher Scientific) using SYBR Premix Ex Taq II (Tli RNaseH Plus; TaKaRa, #RR820A), as previously described (44–46). The following primer sequences used were as follows: KDM6A (forward: 5′-GCGGACAAAAGAAGAACCAG-3′; reverse: 5′-AGATGAGGCGGATGGTAATG-3′), SETD2 (forward: 5′-AAACACAACAACTGAACGAGG-3′; reverse: 5′- GAGTTTGCTT-GTCTGGGTCTC -3′), ARID1A (forward: 5′-CGGCCAATGGATGGCACATA-3′; reverse: 5′-TCGGCCAAACTGGAATGGAA-3′), SMARCA4 (forward: 5′-CTCGGTCCGTCAAAGTGAAGA-3′; reverse: 5′-AGCGGTCCTCCTCTTGTTCC-3′), and ACTB (housekeeping gene) (forward: 5′-AGAGCTACGAGCTGCCTGAC-3′; reverse: 5′-AGCACTGTGTTGGCGTACAG-3′). Relative gene expression was calculated using the ΔΔCt method and normalized to ACTB expression.Western blot analysisWestern blot analysis was performed as previously described (44, 45, 47) with minor modifications. Cell pellets were lysed in buffer containing 0.1 M tris-HCl (pH 7.5), 10% glycerol, and 1% SDS; boiled for 5 min; and centrifuged at 15,000 rpm for 10 min. Protein concentrations were determined using the BCA Protein Assay Kit (Pierce). Equal amounts of protein were separated by SDS–polyacrylamide gel electrophoresis (SDS-PAGE) and transferred onto polyvinylidene difluoride membranes (Millipore). The membranes were blocked with 5% skim milk (Megumilk) or 5% bovine serum albumin (Sigma-Aldrich) in tris-buffered saline containing 0.1% Tween 20 (TBST). They were incubated overnight at 4°C with the following primary antibodies diluted in blocking buffer: anti-ARID1A (1:1000; Cell Signaling Technology, #12354), anti-BRG1 (1:1000; Cell Signaling Technology, #49360), and anti–α-tubulin (1:5000; Sigma-Aldrich, clone B-5-1-2, T5168). After washing three times in TBST, the membranes were incubated with horseradish peroxidase–conjugated secondary antibodies, which included either anti-mouse immunoglobulin G (IgG; 1:5000; Cell Signaling Technology, #7076) or anti-rabbit IgG (1:5000; Cell Signaling Technology, #7074) for 1 hour. Moreover, signals were visualized using the SuperSignal West Femto Maximum Sensitivity Substrate (Thermo Fisher Scientific) and captured with an Odyssey Fc Imaging System (LI-COR).Plasmid constructThe shPseuMO-Tag vector contains a DNA barcode in the 3′ untranslated region of a polyadenylate [poly(A)]–tagged mCherry-PuroR fusion construct, flanked by Tn5 adaptor sequences. This design enables simultaneous capture of the same barcode during 3′ Chromium scRNA-seq (10x Genomics) and ddSEQ scATAC-seq (Bio-Rad) without requiring custom reagents or protocols.The shPseuMO-Tag plasmid was constructed based on the pLenti cytomegalovirus (CMV) green fluorescent protein (GFP) Puro (658-5) vector (Addgene, #17448). The cPPT/CTS, CMV enhancer, CMV promoter, and enhanced GFP regions were removed using HpaI and SalI restriction enzymes. Next, the U6 promoter, shRNA sequence (flanked by BamHI and SalI restriction sites), cPPT/CTS, CMV enhancer, CMV promoter, and a mCherry-P2A-PuroR-Read N1-PCR handle1-Stuffer (for inserting cell barcode sequences)-PCR handle2-Read N2-SV40 poly(A) signal cassette were inserted via In-Fusion 5X HD Cloning Plus (Takara Bio, #638909), using 20– to 30–base pair (bp) homologous sequences, which resulted in shPseuMO-Tag-Stuffer (available upon request). The full-length sequence is provided in table S7.The sequences used for shRNA were as follows: KDM6A (5′-GATGCAAGTCTATGACCAATT-3′; target sequence of predesigned shRNA) (TRCN0000107763, Sigma-Aldrich), SETD2 (5′-AAACCAACAGTCTGTCAGTGTA-3′) (48), ARID1A [5′-GCCTGATCTATCTGGTTCAAT-3′ (ARI3) and 5′-GCATCCTTCCATGAACCAATC-3′ (ARI4) (49)], and SMARCA4 (5′-CGGCAGACACTGTGATCATTT-3′) (50). Nontargeting shRNA (scramble) sequence was used as a negative control (5′-AGTCTTAATCGCGTATAAG-3′) (49). The hairpin sequence used was as follows: 5′-CTGTGAAGCCACAGATGGG-3′ (51).To assemble the cell barcode, based on a slight modification of a previous report (52), a 59-bp oligonucleotide containing a 10-bp random sequence flanked at both ends by a 5-bp HashTag sequence and a reverse extension primer was obtained from Integrated DNA Technologies: 5′-GAGCCTCGTCTCCTGACTNNNNNNNNNNNNNNNNNNNNCGTTGTGAGACGCATGCTGCA-3′. The 5-bp Hash-Tag sequences were as follows: shSCR: ATGCA; shKDM: AGCTG; shSET: TGCTA; shARID: CTGAA; shSMA: GCCAA; shSCR2: ATGCA; shARID3: CGTGC; and shARID4: CTGAA. The following extension reaction was performed to generate double-stranded barcode-shRNA oligonucleotides: 25 μl of NEBNext High-Fidelity 2X PCR Master Mix (NEB, M0541), 1 μl of 100 μM cell barcode, 2 μl of 100 μM reverse extension primer (5′-TGCAGCATGCGTCTCACAACG-3′), and 22 μl of water. The reaction conditions were as follows: 98°C for 2 min, 10× (65°C for 30 s, 72°C for 10 s), 72°C for 2 min, and hold at 4°C. The double-stranded barcode-shRNA oligonucleotide was purified using a QIAquick PCR Purification kit (QIAGEN, 28104). The double-stranded product contained two Bsm BI sites that, upon digestion, generated complementary overhangs for ligation into shPseuMO-Tag-Stuffer. Next, 1.5 μg of BsmBI-v2 digested (New England Biolabs, R0739) shPseuMO-Tag-Stuffer vector was added to a Golden Gate Assembly reaction with the double-stranded barcode insert at a molar ratio of 1:5 and cycled 100× (42°C for 2 min and 16°C for 5 min). The reaction was purified and concentrated in 10 μl of water using the DNA Clean & Concentrator Kit (Zymo, D4033) and transformed into NEB Stable Competent Escherichia coli (New England Biolabs, C3040). Transformants were inoculated into 500 ml of LB medium containing ampicillin (100 μg ml−1) and incubated overnight at 30°C. Bacterial cells were collected by centrifugation at 6000 RCF at 4°C for 15 min, and plasmid DNA was extracted using a QIAGEN Plasmid Plus Maxi kit (QIAGEN, 12943).The PseuMO-Tag vector was constructed by removing the shRNA cassette from the shPseuMO-Tag via HpaI and SalI digestion, followed by a blunting reaction. The PuroR sequence was replaced with a BlastR sequence cloned from lentiCRISPR v2-Blast (Addgene, #83480) using In-Fusion cloning. For barcode construction, a 77-bp oligonucleotide containing an 18-bp random sequence (53) was synthesized: 5′-GAGCCTCGTCTCCTGACTATGCANNNGTNNNCTNNNAGNN NTGNNNCANN NTGCATCGTTGTGAGACGCATGCTGCA-3′, along with the same reverse primer as above. Barcode extension, cloning, and plasmid preparation were performed as described. The full-length sequence is provided in table S7.Lentivirus productionHuman embryonic kidney (HEK) 293T cells were seeded at 3 × 106 cells per 10-cm dish. The following day, 2.5 μg of the lentiviral vector was mixed with 1.25 μg of pCMV-VSVG-RSV/Rev envelope vector and 1.25 μg of pMDLg/pRRE packaging vector in 250 μl of Opti-MEM Reduced Serum Medium (Gibco, 31985-070). FuGENE HD Transfection Reagent (16 μl; Promega, E2311) was added, and the mixture was vortexed, left to incubate for 15 min, and carefully transferred to the HEK293T culture. The medium was refreshed 16 to 24 hours posttransfection, and virus supernatant was collected 48 and 72 hours later, passed through a 0.45-μm filter (Millipore Millex-HV, SLHVR33RS), aliquoted, snap-frozen in liquid nitrogen, and stored at −80°C until further use.Clonal lineage tracing and parallel multiomics profilingTo evaluate intraclonal heterogeneity, BxPC3 cells were seeded at a density of 5000 cells per well in 24-well plates (Figs. 1 to 4). The following day, the cells were transduced with shPseuMO-Tag lentiviral vectors encoding shRNAs targeting ARID1A (ARI3 and ARI4) or a nontargeting control (SCR2) at a multiplicity of infection of 6 to 8 in the presence of polybrene (10 μg/ml). The following day, the transduced cells were subjected to limiting dilution in 96-well plates to establish single cell–derived clones and cultured with puromycin (2 μg/ml; 3 days) to select cells infected with shPseuMO-Tag. Each clone was expanded until it reached ∼1 million cells. The expanded clonal populations were cryopreserved in Bambanker (Nippon Genetics) and stored for subsequent assays. A total of 28 clones (8 SCR2 clones, 9 ARI3 clones, and 11 ARI4 clones) were used in subsequent experiments. Experimental parameters were as follows: number of clones tracked: 28, culturing strategy: isolated single-cell cloning, and expansion time: ∼20 cell divisions.In this single-cell cloning design, a clone was operationally defined as the progeny of a single founder cell isolated by limiting dilution after shPseuMO-Tag transduction. All cells within a clone therefore shared a common post-perturbation ancestor at the time of isolation. The rebarcoding of an established clone provided a finer barcode-defined sublineage resolution among its descendants.Group 3 clones used in downstream functional experiments were selected before those experiments on the basis of high clone-level median GEP3 usage and/or high median peak entropy, together with confirmed ARID1A knockdown. Clones with high GEP3 usage included ARI4#21, ARI4#20, and ARI4#23, whereas clones with high peak entropy included ARI4#23, ARI4#07, ARI4#14, and ARI4#21. ARI4#21, one of the clones with the highest GEP3 usage, was selected for the rebarcoding experiment, with SCR2#04 as the group 2 control. For the AU-15330 experiments, SCR2#01 and SCR2#04 from group 2 and ARI4#14, ARI4#20, ARI4#21, and ARI4#23 from group 3 were analyzed. These experiments were designed to characterize selected high-GEP3 and/or high-entropy clones and were not intended to represent the full range of group 3 behavior.To assess the reproducibility and cell line dependence of ARID1A-associated transcriptional diversification, the shPseuMO-Tag knockdown-and-barcoding workflow was repeated independently in BxPC3 cells and applied to HPAC, SW1990, SUIT-2, and HPAFII cells, as described above under the “Clonal lineage tracing and parallel multiomics profiling” section. Cells were transduced with shPseuMO-Tag lentiviral vectors encoding an ARID1A-targeting or nontargeting control shRNA and selected with puromycin where applicable. Single cell–derived clones were established, expanded, and subjected to downstream single-cell profiling for BxPC3, HPAC, SW1990, and SUIT-2 cells. Because single cell–derived HPAFII clones could not be established, HPAFII cells were analyzed as a pooled population after transduction and selection.Time-course scRNA-seq following ARID1A knockdownTo examine the temporal dynamics of transcriptional diversification after ARID1A depletion, BxPC3 cells were transduced with shPseuMO-Tag lentiviral vectors encoding either a nontargeting control shRNA or ARID1A-targeting shRNAs, as described above. Cells were harvested at day 5 and day 16 after transduction, corresponding ∼2 to 3 and 10 cell divisions, respectively. Viable cells were collected at each time point and subjected to scRNA-seq using the Chromium Single Cell 3′ protocol.The resulting scRNA-seq data were processed using Cell Ranger and Seurat as described below. The transcriptional diversity was quantified using the principal component analysis (PCA)–based diversity index, and transcriptional homogeneity was quantified using NMI as described below. GEP3 module signal was calculated using Seurat’s AddModuleScore() function with the original GEP3 gene set derived from the 28-clone BxPC3 analysis.Clonal lineage tracing and parallel multiomics profilingTo assess heterogeneity among independently perturbed founder lineages, BxPC3 cells were seeded at a density of 5000 cells per well in 24-well plates (Fig. 5). The following day, the cells were transduced with shPseuMO-Tag lentiviral vectors encoding shRNAs targeting KDM6A, SETD2, ARID1A, SMARCA4, or a nontargeting control (Scramble) at a multiplicity of infection of 6 to 8 in the presence of polybrene (10 μg/ml). The next day, 400 transduced BxPC3 cells, representing ∼400 individual clones, were reseeded into 24-well plates and cultured with puromycin (2 μg/ml) for 3 days to select the successfully transduced cells. The cells were expanded until reaching ∼10 million cells. After 19 to 26 days postinfection, the expanded populations were cryopreserved in Bambanker (Nippon Genetics) and stored until subsequent analyses. This procedure was performed independently for each shRNA and resulted in a total of ∼2000 clones analyzed across the five conditions. Experimental parameters were as follows: number of clones tracked: ∼400 clones per shRNA (∼2000 clones in total), culturing strategy: pooled culture, and expansion time: ∼15 cell divisions.In this pooled design, a “clone” denotes the progeny of one of ∼400 independently transduced founder cells per condition, each marked by a distinct PseuMO-Tag barcode; differences measured across these barcodes therefore reflect interclonal heterogeneity among independently perturbed founders rather than diversification within a single lineage.Analytical characterization of GEP coherence and transcriptional dispersioncNMF usage values were normalized to sum to one within each cell. For each GEP, cells with nonzero usage were ranked according to their usage values, and cells in the top 5% were selected. Up to 100 cells were randomly sampled from this population in each of 200 iterations. Cell-cell similarity was calculated using the top 20 genes associated with each GEP as the median pairwise Pearson correlation between sampled cells. Gene-gene coexpression was calculated as the median pairwise Pearson correlation between the same top-ranked genes across sampled cells; genes with no variance among the sampled cells were excluded from the correlation calculation.To evaluate gene-module coherence across different levels of GEP3 usage, GEP3-positive cells were divided into five percentile bins: 0 to 25, 25 to 50, 50 to 75, 75 to 95, and 95 to 100%. Equal numbers of cells, determined by the smallest bin and capped at 100 cells, were randomly sampled from each bin in each of 200 iterations. full_text_sections.results: RESULTSLoss of EMs promotes transcriptional heterogeneity in pancreatic cancerLoss-of-function alterations in EMs are frequent across human cancers, including PDAC (22, 35). Given their essential role in maintaining chromatin organization and transcriptional fidelity (18), we reasoned that impaired epigenetic regulation—whether through mutation or reduced expression—might contribute to tumor heterogeneity. Analyzing RNA sequencing (RNA-seq) data from The Cancer Genome Atlas (TCGA) pancreatic adenocarcinoma cohort, we quantified transcriptomic diversity across tumors using Shannon entropy (32) and principal component–based diversity indices (36). The reduced expression of EMs was associated with higher transcriptomic diversity for most of the modifiers tested (209 and 136 of 240 modifiers for the two metrics, respectively; fig. S1, A to D). This broad correlation links reduced EM expression to tumor transcriptional diversity at the population level but cannot establish causality or resolve events within individual tumors, motivating a controlled, clone-resolved perturbation approach.To test directly whether EM loss promotes transcriptomic heterogeneity, we developed shPseuMO-Tag, an all-in-one DNA barcoding system that couples genetic perturbation and lineage tracing with single-cell multimodal profiling (fig. S2, A and B). We applied it to the PDAC cell lines BxPC3 and HPAFII, targeting four EMs (ARID1A, KDM6A, SETD2, and SMARCA4), chosen because their reduced expression correlates with transcriptomic diversity (fig. S1, C and D) and because they are recurrently inactivated in PDAC and associated with poor prognosis (23–28). To avoid batch effects, all knockdown conditions across both cell lines were pooled and processed in a single single-cell RNA-seq (scRNA-seq) run (37). The knockdown of these modifiers increased transcriptomic heterogeneity, measured by normalized mutual information (NMI) (figs. S1, E to H and fig. S2C; see Materials and Methods) (4, 38). Together with the clinical correlation, these results are consistent with a causal contribution of EM loss to transcriptional diversification in PDAC.Clonal lineage tracing and parallel multiomics profiling reveal transcriptional heterogeneity following ARID1A lossWhile our initial screen indicated that EM loss promotes transcriptional heterogeneity (fig. S1, A to H), it remained unclear whether a heterogeneous population can emerge from a single cell following loss of an EM. We focused on ARID1A, a key subunit of the SWI/SNF chromatin-remodeling complex frequently inactivated in PDAC (18, 39). Using shPseuMO-Tag targeting ARID1A (two independent shRNAs, ARI3# and ARI4#) or a nontargeting control (SCR2#), we transduced BxPC3 cells and, after single-cell cloning and ∼20 cell divisions, established 28 clonal populations (8 control and 20 ARID1A-knockdown clones; Fig. 1A, fig. S3A, and see text S1). Analyzing multiple independent clones from the same parental population, ARID1A-deficient clones showed broader morphological diversity and more variable and generally reduced growth relative to controls (fig. S3, B and C), indicating that ARID1A deficiency increases phenotypic heterogeneity among independently derived clones.Fig. 1.Clonal lineage tracing and parallel multiomics profiling reveal transcriptional heterogeneity following ARID1A loss.(A) Clone-resolved workflow. BxPC3 cells were transduced with control or two shARID1A constructs, isolated by single-cell cloning, expanded for approximately 20 divisions, pooled for parallel scRNA-seq and scATAC-seq, with selected clones retained for functional assays. (B) UMAP projections of 15,369 scRNA-seq cells from 28 clones, colored by shRNA condition, transcriptomic cluster, or clone identity. (C) Fractional distribution of transcriptomic clusters within each clone; numbers indicate assigned cells. (D and E) NMI-based transcriptional homogeneity for pooled conditions (D) and individual clones (E). Violin plots show bootstrap distributions; labels indicate mean ± SD, and the dashed line indicates the control-clone median. ***P < 0.001, one-way ANOVA with Dunnett’s post hoc test. (F) UMAP projections colored by GEP1–GEP7 usage. (G) MSigDB Hallmark 2020 enrichment among GEP-associated genes; dot size indicates gene ratio and color indicates adjusted P value. (H) GEP usage in 100 sampled cells per clone.
