full_text_sections.discussion: DISCUSSIONA central challenge in cancer biology is to understand how transcriptional heterogeneity arises and is organized within tumors (3, 5, 11–16). Recent surveys have cataloged recurrent expression programs across tumors and shown that the states available to cancer cells are strongly context-dependent (5). Here, by coupling barcoded perturbation with clone-resolved multiomics, we found that loss of a single EM, ARID1A, increases transcriptional variability both among the descendants of a single founder cell and between independently derived clones. Programs with defined signatures, such as EMT-like and interferon-like programs, were also represented among ARID1A-deficient clones; however, in the independent BxPC3 replicate, they were not specific to knockdown and also appeared in controls—consistent with ARID1A loss relaxing constraints on pre-existing states rather than creating new ones. The feature that recurred most consistently in association with ARID1A loss was GEP3—a cNMF-derived component that corresponded to no dominant pathway signature and whose high-usage cells were less similar to one another than those of the coherent programs. These observations suggest that GEP3 may be better understood not as a discrete cell state but as a recurrent axis of transcriptional variability associated with ARID1A loss.Such an interpretation would have implications for how components of this kind are interpreted. Factorization methods such as cNMF are generally used to identify coordinated modules, and a factor reflecting variability rather than coordination would lack both a dominant signature and a coherent set of coexpressing cells—features that might invite its dismissal as a residual or technical artifact. Several observations argue against that reading here: the principal properties of GEP3 were recovered in an independent BxPC3 experiment; related signature-poor components were observed in some additional cell lines; the observed combination of gene weights and clone-level association was not reproduced by the expression-shuffling procedure used here; and GEP3 usage was associated with both chromatin-accessibility variability and clone-level phenotypes. We note, however, that because GEP3 lacks a defining signature, its correspondence across cell lines rests on shared statistical properties rather than on gene identity—a weaker form of correspondence than for signature-defined programs, and one we present as such. Whether variability-associated factors of this kind arise more generally after perturbations that relax transcriptional constraints will require dedicated investigation.The chromatin data suggest how this variability may be related to chromatin remodeling and what sustains the associated features. ARID1A loss did not establish new clone-specific chromatin identities but relaxed existing constraints, broadening accessibility at otherwise silenced, lineage-inappropriate loci while remaining largely within annotated regulatory elements. This partial derepression was accompanied by elevated peak entropy, which, measured in an independent modality, tracked with GEP3 usage rather than with transcriptional heterogeneity in general. Notably, this variability was not simply a passive consequence of losing a chromatin remodeler: degrading SMARCA4 reduced both GEP3 usage and the chromatin-accessibility entropy associated with it. This suggests that residual SWI/SNF activity does not merely fail to restrain the genome but actively participates in maintaining the derepressed landscape that ARID1A loss creates—a role consistent with reports that ARID1A-deficient cells assemble alternative cBAF complexes incorporating ARID1B, which compensate incompletely (42, 43), and with the buffering of chromatin perturbations by functionally coupled remodelers.What such variability might offer a tumor is suggested by the pattern of selection we observed, although our data do not establish the underlying mechanism directly. Clones with high baseline GEP3 usage showed no growth advantage under standard conditions, and ARID1A-deficient clones proliferated more slowly than controls. Preferential recovery was observed only under selection and only under some pressures: GEP3-enriched clones were favored under hypoxia-mimetic and glutamine-deprived conditions and during lung colonization, whereas glucose deprivation instead favored interferon-like and EMT-like clones. This context dependence is compatible with a bet-hedging–like model, in which maintaining a range of transcriptional profiles carries a cost under stable conditions but can pay off when conditions change. Such a model is intrinsically defined at the level of populations rather than of single cells—the relevant property is the range of profiles a lineage can access—which matches the clonal resolution of our lineage-tracing system. Consistent with this view, lung-engrafted populations derived from GEP3-enriched clones were no longer organized primarily by a GEP3-like component but by a lung-associated adaptive program, as were the few control clones that engrafted; nevertheless, GEP3 module scores were retained. Cells of different clonal origins were thus organized by a shared adaptive state under selection, consistent with the possibility that high baseline GEP3 usage marks clonal populations from which environment-specific states can emerge, rather than cells committed to a particular state.This raises a question about how this variability has previously been described. EMT has long been linked to phenotypic plasticity, and the EMT-like GEP1 was indeed transcriptionally variable in our data (Fig. 1E)—yet GEP3, which lacks a defining signature, was more variable still. Intermediate or partial EMT states are themselves defined by mixed, low-specificity signatures, which makes them difficult to distinguish from a signature-poor, high-variability component such as GEP3 (GEP1, but not GEP3, showed a weak trend toward enrichment for curated partial-EMT signatures; fig. S4K). It is therefore conceivable that some of the plasticity historically attributed to intermediate EMT reflects an unrecognized contribution from GEP3-like variability that was grouped with EMT in the absence of distinguishing markers. This possibility is speculative, but it suggests that marker-independent, clone-resolved approaches may be needed to separate the two.Our study leaves several questions open. Selection was measured at the level of GEP3-enriched clones, and we could not determine which cells within such a clone were the ones actually selected under a given pressure; addressing this would require lineage tracing at finer resolution than our current system provides. The factors that bias a given ARID1A-deficient clone toward a GEP3-high regime rather than toward an EMT- or interferon-dominant program also remain unknown. Last, one cell line, SUIT-2, did not show increased heterogeneity after ARID1A knockdown. SUIT-2 carries a truncating ARID1A mutation and may have adapted chronically to reduced ARID1A function, unlike the wild-type lines examined after acute knockdown; because chronic adaptation was not tested directly, this interpretation remains speculative, and we cannot exclude that the response to ARID1A loss depends on molecular context in ways not captured here.Together, our findings suggest that EM loss may contribute to tumor evolution less by installing a new phenotype than by widening the range of phenotypes a lineage can reach. ARID1A loss did not push cells into a defined malignant state; rather, it appeared to lift constraints, with residual remodeling activity helping to hold the resulting landscape open. Clone-resolved perturbation makes this process visible and suggests that an important part of what epigenetic disruption produces may be not a state to be cataloged, but variability itself.
full_text_sections.other: INTRODUCTIONIntratumoral heterogeneity (ITH) in gene expression and cell states is a defining feature of cancer and a major determinant of malignant progression, therapeutic resistance, and recurrence (1–6). Tumors are increasingly viewed as dynamic systems composed of diverse and evolving cellular states rather than uniform populations of genetically identical cells (7–10). How this transcriptional heterogeneity arises and how it is organized within tumors remains a central challenge in cancer biology (3, 5, 11–16).Epigenetic modifiers (EMs) are strong candidates for shaping this heterogeneity (17–21). Large-scale sequencing has revealed recurrent loss-of-function mutations in chromatin remodelers, histone modifiers, and other chromatin-associated factors across many cancers (22). In pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma (PDAC), inactivating mutations in EMs such as ARID1A, SMARCA4, KDM6A, and SETD2 are frequent (23–28) and often arise as late events, suggesting that they act less as classical oncogenic drivers than as modulators of tumor phenotype.Because EMs constrain and coordinate transcriptional programs, their loss is expected to relax transcriptional control and increase variability in gene expression (17, 20, 29–31). However, most analyses to date have relied on bulk or population-level single-cell profiling, which cannot determine how EM loss reshapes heterogeneity within individual clonal lineages. It therefore remains unclear whether EM loss simply increases stochastic transcriptional noise or instead drives defined modes of transcriptional diversification.Critically, the consequences of EM loss need not be uniform across cells. Individual cancer cells differ in transcriptional state, chromatin landscape, and regulatory context at the time of perturbation (32–34), so loss of a single regulator may produce divergent outcomes in different cells of an otherwise genetically homogeneous population. Population-level analyses cannot distinguish whether the resulting heterogeneity reflects pre-existing differences, stochastic variation, or divergent responses to a shared perturbation. Resolving these possibilities requires strategies that track the transcriptional consequences of EM loss within defined clonal lineages.To this end, we developed shPseuMO-Tag (shRNA-equipped pseudo-multiomics and cell tagging), a barcoded short hairpin RNA (shRNA) system that couples gene knockdown with clonal lineage tracing and parallel single-cell multiomic profiling. Applying it to ARID1A in PDAC cells, we found that ARID1A deficiency increased transcriptional variability across many clonal lineages. A recurrent consensus non-negative matrix factorization (cNMF)–derived component termed GEP3 lacked a dominant pathway annotation, and cells with high GEP3 usage showed low mutual similarity, supporting its interpretation as an axis of transcriptional variability rather than a discrete cell state. Across clones, GEP3 usage was associated with chromatin-accessibility variability, and both GEP3 usage and accessibility entropy were reduced by SMARCA4 degradation. Clones with high baseline GEP3 usage were preferentially recovered under selected environmental stress conditions and after lung colonization. Together, these findings suggest that ARID1A loss widens the range of transcriptional phenotypes accessible to a lineage and highlight the value of clone-resolved perturbation for dissecting how epigenetic alterations shape ITH. Loss of EMs promotes transcriptional heterogeneity in pancreatic cancerLoss-of-function alterations in EMs are frequent across human cancers, including PDAC (22, 35). Given their essential role in maintaining chromatin organization and transcriptional fidelity (18), we reasoned that impaired epigenetic regulation—whether through mutation or reduced expression—might contribute to tumor heterogeneity. Analyzing RNA sequencing (RNA-seq) data from The Cancer Genome Atlas (TCGA) pancreatic adenocarcinoma cohort, we quantified transcriptomic diversity across tumors using Shannon entropy (32) and principal component–based diversity indices (36). The reduced expression of EMs was associated with higher transcriptomic diversity for most of the modifiers tested (209 and 136 of 240 modifiers for the two metrics, respectively; fig. S1, A to D). This broad correlation links reduced EM expression to tumor transcriptional diversity at the population level but cannot establish causality or resolve events within individual tumors, motivating a controlled, clone-resolved perturbation approach.To test directly whether EM loss promotes transcriptomic heterogeneity, we developed shPseuMO-Tag, an all-in-one DNA barcoding system that couples genetic perturbation and lineage tracing with single-cell multimodal profiling (fig. S2, A and B). We applied it to the PDAC cell lines BxPC3 and HPAFII, targeting four EMs (ARID1A, KDM6A, SETD2, and SMARCA4), chosen because their reduced expression correlates with transcriptomic diversity (fig. S1, C and D) and because they are recurrently inactivated in PDAC and associated with poor prognosis (23–28). To avoid batch effects, all knockdown conditions across both cell lines were pooled and processed in a single single-cell RNA-seq (scRNA-seq) run (37). The knockdown of these modifiers increased transcriptomic heterogeneity, measured by normalized mutual information (NMI) (figs. S1, E to H and fig. S2C; see Materials and Methods) (4, 38). Together with the clinical correlation, these results are consistent with a causal contribution of EM loss to transcriptional diversification in PDAC. Clonal lineage tracing and parallel multiomics profiling reveal transcriptional heterogeneity following ARID1A lossWhile our initial screen indicated that EM loss promotes transcriptional heterogeneity (fig. S1, A to H), it remained unclear whether a heterogeneous population can emerge from a single cell following loss of an EM. We focused on ARID1A, a key subunit of the SWI/SNF chromatin-remodeling complex frequently inactivated in PDAC (18, 39). Using shPseuMO-Tag targeting ARID1A (two independent shRNAs, ARI3# and ARI4#) or a nontargeting control (SCR2#), we transduced BxPC3 cells and, after single-cell cloning and ∼20 cell divisions, established 28 clonal populations (8 control and 20 ARID1A-knockdown clones; Fig. 1A, fig. S3A, and see text S1). Analyzing multiple independent clones from the same parental population, ARID1A-deficient clones showed broader morphological diversity and more variable and generally reduced growth relative to controls (fig. full_text: AbstractSeptic pulmonary embolism (SPE) is a rare complication of peripherally inserted central catheters (PICC), with few neonatal reports. We present a premature infant who developed recurrent apnea and hypoxemia during PICC indwelling. Imaging revealed bilateral thick-walled cavitary lesions. Although two consecutive conventional peripheral blood cultures remained negative, MSSA was identified from PICC tip culture, deep sputum culture, and NGS analysis of peripheral blood, PICC intraluminal blood, and deep sputum samples. The infant recovered after 39 days of antimicrobial therapy, including five weeks of targeted linezolid. This case suggests that PICC surface biofilms were the most probable source of septic emboli causing occult SPE, underscoring the importance of considering catheter-related pulmonary embolism in neonates with unexplained respiratory deterioration.Keywords: neonate, next-generation sequencing, peripherally inserted central catheter, pulmonary abscess, septic pulmonary embolism 3.DiscussionSeptic pulmonary embolism is a critical condition caused by infected thromboemboli obstructing the pulmonary arteries, leading to suppurative infection and infarction. Its clinical presentation is often nonspecific and can mimic pneumonia, making diagnosis challenging (9). SPE is rare in children and even more uncommon in neonates; due to its subtle symptoms, it is frequently missed or misdiagnosed, and its true incidence is likely underestimated. The diagnosis of SPE was established based on the criteria proposed by Cook et al. (10), and our case met all four criteria: (1) CT findings of bilateral peripheral thick-walled cavitary nodules; (2) PICC tip culture positive for MSSA, with NGS confirming the same organism in PICC and peripheral blood; (3) negative peripheral blood cultures, no vegetations on echocardiography, and negative testing for other pathogens (including tuberculosis, viruses, and fungi); (4) complete clinical and radiographic recovery after 35 days (5 weeks) of targeted linezolid therapy, preceded by 4 days of empirical vancomycin (total 39 days).The characteristic imaging findings of large, thick-walled cavities may be attributed to the unique anatomical features of neonatal pulmonary vasculature. The small caliber of peripheral pulmonary arteries predisposes to the entrapment of septic emboli, leading to localized infarction and abscess formation (11, 12). This case emphasized that pulmonary imaging enables early detection of this rare complication in neonates with a history of central venous catheterization who present with unexplained respiratory deterioration (13). From an infectious microbiology perspective, the fact that both catheter-related NGS and cultures were positive revealed that PICC biofilms might serve as an occult infectious reservoir, with dislodged septic emboli causing focal pulmonary lesions but not leading to systemic bloodstream infection.In this case, NGS was used as an adjunctive diagnostic tool and demonstrated its unique value (14). By directly detecting pathogen nucleic acids, NGS provided results within 24 h, substantially faster than conventional culture methods, facilitating early pathogen identification and targeted therapy. Particularly in this premature, low birth weight infant, early and precise diagnosis was critical for guiding effective antimicrobial treatment. Although β-lactams are first line agents for confirmed MSSA infections, vancomycin was chosen empirically at symptom onset because the causative pathogen was unknown and the infant had multiple risk factors (prematurity, low birth weight, central venous catheterization), considering the local infection epidemiology. Despite rapid microbiological confirmation of MSSA, the infant showed no clinical improvement, and vancomycin trough concentrations remained subtherapeutic despite dose adjustments, reflecting interindividual pharmacokinetic variability in neonates, particularly extremely low birth weight infants. This finding highlights the need for close therapeutic drug monitoring when vancomycin is used in this population. Subsequent switch to linezolid resulted in clinical and radiographic improvement. Furthermore, the negative lumbar puncture findings excluded meningitis at the time of presentation, supporting that the pulmonary lesions were the primary septic focus without concomitant central nervous system infection. Subsequent switch to linezolid resulted in clinical and radiographic improvement. We do not claim failure of β-lactam therapy, as these agents were not administered. Instead, the decision to use the prolonged IV-to-oral linezolid regimen was based on our institutional experience and established antimicrobial stewardship protocol, which favors linezolid for severe catheter-related MSSA infections in extremely preterm infants, particularly when prolonged parenteral access is impractical. This individualized approach, reached after multidisciplinary assessment, does not imply that linezolid should replace β-lactams as standard first-line therapy for MSSA. This underscores the importance of timely diagnosis, early recognition of risk factors, and adequate antimicrobial therapy in the management this situation.Several differential diagnoses were considered and excluded. Severe necrotizing pneumonia (15–17) typically presents with consolidative, lobar, or segmental distribution, whereas the bilateral, multifocal, randomly distributed peripheral thick-walled cavities in our case suggest hematogenous dissemination (18). Although direct embolic evidence was lacking, the presence of a probable intravascular source (positive PICC culture), bilateral randomly distributed pulmonary lesions, and exclusion of other embolic sources support SPE as the most plausible mechanism (19, 20). Fungal infection and other causes of neonatal cavitary lung disease were ruled out by negative screening tests.This report has several limitations. The diagnosis of SPE was clinicoradiological without histopathological or angiographic confirmation. Additionally, the entire catheterized venous pathway was not systematically assessed by Doppler ultrasound, which might have provided further evidence regarding the source of emboli. Negative conventional blood cultures raise the possibility that NGS detected bacterial DNAemia rather than true bacteremia. A positive PICC-tip culture may reflect colonization rather than true infection, as semiquantitative culture or differential time-to-positivity was not performed. Finally, NGS cannot establish clonal identity; without molecular strain-typing, we cannot prove that the PICC and pulmonary isolates originated from the same strain. These factors collectively temper the certainty of our conclusions. 4.ConclusionThis study reports a rare case of bilateral pulmonary abscesses secondary to presumed PICC-related septic pulmonary embolism in an extremely low birth weight infant. Microbiological evidence suggested that the PICC surface biofilm was the most probable source of septic emboli, leading to localized pulmonary infection without concurrent systemic bacteremia. This case highlights that SPE should be considered in the differential diagnosis for neonates with indwelling PICC who present with unexplained respiratory deterioration. Contrast-enhanced chest CT, combined with comprehensive pathogen detection (including NGS), facilitates early diagnosis and targeted therapy. Furthermore, these findings underscore the need for rigorous PICC maintenance and infection control strategies in the NICU to minimize biofilm formation and mitigate the risk of such severe complications. 1.IntroductionSeptic pulmonary embolism (SPE) (1) is a critical condition resulting from infected thrombi lodging in the pulmonary arteries, causing pulmonary infarction, vasculitis, and tissue necrosis. In adults, SPE is commonly associated with intravenous drug abuse, central venous catheters, infective endocarditis, and deep tissue infections; while in children, the incidence is lower and typically secondary to underlying diseases or medical interventions (2). S. aureus and Candida species are the predominant pathogens, with strong invasiveness leading to vascular damage and distant dissemination (3, 4). Clinically, SPE often presents with non-specific symptoms such as fever and cough and is frequently mistaken for common pneumonia. However, delayed intervention can rapidly progress to life-threatening complications, including necrotizing pneumonia and septic shock, and is associated with high mortality (5). Therefore, early recognition and precise intervention are essential. Central venous catheters are widely used in critically ill neonates, and common complications such as catheter obstruction, local infection, and catheter-related bloodstream infection have received considerable clinical attention (6). However, catheter-associated SPE is rarely reported owing to its low incidence. Here we present a case of presumed SPE associated with PICC-related methicillin-susceptible S. aureus infection, which progressed to bilateral pulmonary abscesses in an extremely low birth weight infant, aiming to provide a clinical reference for the early identification and precise management of this rare complication. 2.Case reportA female infant delivered by cesarean section at 27 weeks and 6 days of gestation had a birth weight of 990 g (10th percentile) and Apgar scores of 5 at 1 min and 7 at 5 min. She was admitted to the neonatal intensive care unit (NICU) immediately after birth due to respiratory distress, and received nasal Continuous Positive Airway Pressure (nCPAP) and parenteral nutrition. Enteral feeding was initiated on day 1 but was poorly tolerated, presenting with vomiting and abdominal distension. An umbilical venous catheter (UVC) was placed for the first 7 days. On postnatal day 8, the UVC was removed and replaced with a peripherally inserted central catheter (PICC). Under color Doppler ultrasound guidance, the PICC was inserted via the superficial temporal and external jugular veins into the subclavian vein and subsequently into the superior vena cava, without complications (Figure 1A). After admission, the infant's respiratory status gradually improved, and oxygen delivery was stepped down from nCPAP to heated humidified nasal cannula (HHNC, FiO2 25%, flow 4 L/min), with stable oxygen saturation. On day 14 after PICC insertion (postnatal day 21), the infant developed 3-5 apneic episodes per hour with hypoxemia (SpO2 < 85%), requiring an increase in FiO2 to 40%–50%, and escalation of respiratory support from HHNC to nCPAP (PEEP 6–8 cmH2O), accompanied by lethargy, poor responsiveness, and reduced limb tone.Figure 1Imaging findings of the infant. (A) Chest x-ray (PICC day 8, postnatal day 16): Proper PICC placement. (B) Chest x-ray (PICC day 14, postnatal day 21, onset of clinical symptoms): Patchy consolidations in both lungs with thick-walled cavities. (C) C1-2-3: Contrast-enhanced chest CT(1 day after clinical onset, postnatal day 22): Bilateral pneumonia with lung abscess formation (C-1: coronal view; C-2 and C-3: axial views at different levels). (D) Chest x-ray (treated with 4 days vancomycin and 1 day linezolid, postnatal day26): Slight progression of the right-sided lesion. (E) Chest x-ray (1week after drug discontinuation, postnatal day 67): Significant absorption of lung lesions and reduction in cavity size. (F) Chest x-ray (2 months after treatment discontinuation): No obvious abnormalities.Panel A shows a pediatric chest X-ray with an arrow indicating increased opacity along the mediastinum. Panel B displays an X-ray with arrows highlighting abnormal densities in the lower right lung. Panel C-1 is a coronal CT scan with arrows pointing to bilateral lung lesions. Panel C-2 and C-3 are axial CT scans with arrows identifying round lesions in both lungs. Panel D presents a chest X-ray with bilateral opacities marked by arrows. Panel E shows a chest X-ray with a mediastinal opacity indicated. Panel F features a chest X-ray demonstrating subtle parenchymal changes marked by an arrow.Chest x-ray revealed bilateral diffuse patchy consolidations with thick-walled cavities and surrounding exudative changes, suggestive of bilateral pulmonary abscesses. Contrast-enhanced chest CT showed: 1 multiple bilateral thick-walled cavitary lesions, with the largest measuring approximately 14.7 mm × 10.2 mm in the right lung and 20.3 mm × 12.1 mm in the left lung, with slightly irregular inner walls and patchy peripheral exudative opacities (Figure 1); 2 a well-defined, round nodule (approximately 3 mm) in the periphery of the right lung without significant contrast enhancement; 3 dense consolidation in both lower lobes with thickened and distorted pulmonary markings; and 4 localized emphysema in the left lower lobe. Laboratory parameters showed a peripheral leukocyte count was 21.11 × 109/L (reference range: 5.0–20.0 × 109/L), with neutrophils count was 15.54 × 109/L (reference range: 2.0–10.0 × 109/L); platelet count was 299 × 109/L (reference: 242–378 × 109/L); C-reactive protein (CRP) was 4.3 mg/L (reference: 0–3 mg/L). Serum 1,3-β D-glucan (G-test), galactomannan (GM-test), T-SPOT, TB assay, and nucleic acid testing for respiratory syncytial virus, adenovirus, influenza virus, and parainfluenza virus were all negative. Ultrasound of the heart and the vessels showed no obvious vegetation or thrombus formation. To exclude central nervous system involvement, a lumbar puncture was performed on postnatal day 21 prior to antibiotic administration. CSF analysis showed normal cell count and differential, protein, chloride, glucose, and negative bacterial culture, effectively ruling out meningitis.Microbiological Findings including: 1 Peripheral blood culture: 2 consecutive samples were negative; 2 PICC tip and deep sputum cultures: methicillin-susceptible S. aureus (MSSA) was isolated; 3 Next-generation sequencing (NGS): using the Illumina NovaSeq 6,000 platform. Samples (peripheral blood, PICC intraluminal blood, and deep sputum) were collected at the onset of clinical deterioration (PICC day 14, postnatal day 21), before the initiation of antibiotic therapy. Deep sputum specimens were obtained by passing a sterile suction catheter through the nasal cavity into the lower airway under aseptic conditions, with suction applied only after the catheter had bypassed the oropharynx to minimize upper-airway contamination. The procedure was performed by experienced neonatal nurse. Each sequencing run included sterile water as a negative control, and no microbial reads were detected in these controls. The validated detection threshold for a positive call was defined as ≥5 specific reads mapping to a given pathogen at the genus or species level, with a relative abundance of ≥0.5% after stringent host-background subtraction (removal of human reads). This threshold was established and validated by the performing laboratory through serial dilution experiments using reference strains (including S. aureus, E. coli, and C. albicans) spiked into negative clinical matrices at varying concentrations to determine the limit of detection, following the general principles outlined in the expert consensus on the clinical application of metagenomic next-generation sequencing for pathogen detection (7). The ≥5 read count threshold was chosen to balance sensitivity and specificity by minimizing false-positive calls from low-level background noise or reagent contamination, while the ≥0.5% relative abundance criterion helped distinguish true pathogens from commensal or environmental organisms (8). Clinical significance was assigned when the same pathogen was concordantly detected in at least two distinct sample types in the context of compatible clinical and imaging findings. After rigorous host-background subtraction and quality filtering, S. aureus was detected in all three specimen types with concordant signals (specific read counts: 156 in peripheral blood, 243 in PICC intraluminal blood, and 892 in deep sputum; relative abundance >5% in each specimen). Antimicrobial susceptibility testing showed that the isolate was mecA gene-negative and susceptible to cefoxitin, linezolid, and vancomycin, confirming MSSA as the causative pathogen.The PICC was removed immediately after microbiological sampling on postnatal day 21, before the initiation of antimicrobial therapy. The infant initially received vancomycin for 4 days, with the dose escalated from 15 mg/kg to 20 mg/kg every 12 h. However, trough concentrations remained subtherapeutic (3.06 μg/mL and 3.78 μg/mL, respectively), and the infant showed no clinical improvement; pulmonary lesions progressed radiographically. full_text_sections.abstract: AbstractSeptic pulmonary embolism (SPE) is a rare complication of peripherally inserted central catheters (PICC), with few neonatal reports. We present a premature infant who developed recurrent apnea and hypoxemia during PICC indwelling. Imaging revealed bilateral thick-walled cavitary lesions. Although two consecutive conventional peripheral blood cultures remained negative, MSSA was identified from PICC tip culture, deep sputum culture, and NGS analysis of peripheral blood, PICC intraluminal blood, and deep sputum samples. The infant recovered after 39 days of antimicrobial therapy, including five weeks of targeted linezolid. This case suggests that PICC surface biofilms were the most probable source of septic emboli causing occult SPE, underscoring the importance of considering catheter-related pulmonary embolism in neonates with unexplained respiratory deterioration.Keywords: neonate, next-generation sequencing, peripherally inserted central catheter, pulmonary abscess, septic pulmonary embolism
full_text_sections.discussion: 3.DiscussionSeptic pulmonary embolism is a critical condition caused by infected thromboemboli obstructing the pulmonary arteries, leading to suppurative infection and infarction. Its clinical presentation is often nonspecific and can mimic pneumonia, making diagnosis challenging (9). SPE is rare in children and even more uncommon in neonates; due to its subtle symptoms, it is frequently missed or misdiagnosed, and its true incidence is likely underestimated. The diagnosis of SPE was established based on the criteria proposed by Cook et al. (10), and our case met all four criteria: (1) CT findings of bilateral peripheral thick-walled cavitary nodules; (2) PICC tip culture positive for MSSA, with NGS confirming the same organism in PICC and peripheral blood; (3) negative peripheral blood cultures, no vegetations on echocardiography, and negative testing for other pathogens (including tuberculosis, viruses, and fungi); (4) complete clinical and radiographic recovery after 35 days (5 weeks) of targeted linezolid therapy, preceded by 4 days of empirical vancomycin (total 39 days).The characteristic imaging findings of large, thick-walled cavities may be attributed to the unique anatomical features of neonatal pulmonary vasculature. The small caliber of peripheral pulmonary arteries predisposes to the entrapment of septic emboli, leading to localized infarction and abscess formation (11, 12). This case emphasized that pulmonary imaging enables early detection of this rare complication in neonates with a history of central venous catheterization who present with unexplained respiratory deterioration (13). From an infectious microbiology perspective, the fact that both catheter-related NGS and cultures were positive revealed that PICC biofilms might serve as an occult infectious reservoir, with dislodged septic emboli causing focal pulmonary lesions but not leading to systemic bloodstream infection.In this case, NGS was used as an adjunctive diagnostic tool and demonstrated its unique value (14). By directly detecting pathogen nucleic acids, NGS provided results within 24 h, substantially faster than conventional culture methods, facilitating early pathogen identification and targeted therapy. Particularly in this premature, low birth weight infant, early and precise diagnosis was critical for guiding effective antimicrobial treatment. Although β-lactams are first line agents for confirmed MSSA infections, vancomycin was chosen empirically at symptom onset because the causative pathogen was unknown and the infant had multiple risk factors (prematurity, low birth weight, central venous catheterization), considering the local infection epidemiology. Despite rapid microbiological confirmation of MSSA, the infant showed no clinical improvement, and vancomycin trough concentrations remained subtherapeutic despite dose adjustments, reflecting interindividual pharmacokinetic variability in neonates, particularly extremely low birth weight infants. This finding highlights the need for close therapeutic drug monitoring when vancomycin is used in this population. Subsequent switch to linezolid resulted in clinical and radiographic improvement. Furthermore, the negative lumbar puncture findings excluded meningitis at the time of presentation, supporting that the pulmonary lesions were the primary septic focus without concomitant central nervous system infection. Subsequent switch to linezolid resulted in clinical and radiographic improvement. We do not claim failure of β-lactam therapy, as these agents were not administered. Instead, the decision to use the prolonged IV-to-oral linezolid regimen was based on our institutional experience and established antimicrobial stewardship protocol, which favors linezolid for severe catheter-related MSSA infections in extremely preterm infants, particularly when prolonged parenteral access is impractical. This individualized approach, reached after multidisciplinary assessment, does not imply that linezolid should replace β-lactams as standard first-line therapy for MSSA. This underscores the importance of timely diagnosis, early recognition of risk factors, and adequate antimicrobial therapy in the management this situation.Several differential diagnoses were considered and excluded. Severe necrotizing pneumonia (15–17) typically presents with consolidative, lobar, or segmental distribution, whereas the bilateral, multifocal, randomly distributed peripheral thick-walled cavities in our case suggest hematogenous dissemination (18). Although direct embolic evidence was lacking, the presence of a probable intravascular source (positive PICC culture), bilateral randomly distributed pulmonary lesions, and exclusion of other embolic sources support SPE as the most plausible mechanism (19, 20). Fungal infection and other causes of neonatal cavitary lung disease were ruled out by negative screening tests.This report has several limitations. The diagnosis of SPE was clinicoradiological without histopathological or angiographic confirmation. Additionally, the entire catheterized venous pathway was not systematically assessed by Doppler ultrasound, which might have provided further evidence regarding the source of emboli. Negative conventional blood cultures raise the possibility that NGS detected bacterial DNAemia rather than true bacteremia. A positive PICC-tip culture may reflect colonization rather than true infection, as semiquantitative culture or differential time-to-positivity was not performed. Finally, NGS cannot establish clonal identity; without molecular strain-typing, we cannot prove that the PICC and pulmonary isolates originated from the same strain. These factors collectively temper the certainty of our conclusions.
full_text_sections.conclusion: 4.ConclusionThis study reports a rare case of bilateral pulmonary abscesses secondary to presumed PICC-related septic pulmonary embolism in an extremely low birth weight infant. Microbiological evidence suggested that the PICC surface biofilm was the most probable source of septic emboli, leading to localized pulmonary infection without concurrent systemic bacteremia. This case highlights that SPE should be considered in the differential diagnosis for neonates with indwelling PICC who present with unexplained respiratory deterioration. Contrast-enhanced chest CT, combined with comprehensive pathogen detection (including NGS), facilitates early diagnosis and targeted therapy. Furthermore, these findings underscore the need for rigorous PICC maintenance and infection control strategies in the NICU to minimize biofilm formation and mitigate the risk of such severe complications.
full_text_sections.other: 1.IntroductionSeptic pulmonary embolism (SPE) (1) is a critical condition resulting from infected thrombi lodging in the pulmonary arteries, causing pulmonary infarction, vasculitis, and tissue necrosis. In adults, SPE is commonly associated with intravenous drug abuse, central venous catheters, infective endocarditis, and deep tissue infections; while in children, the incidence is lower and typically secondary to underlying diseases or medical interventions (2). S. aureus and Candida species are the predominant pathogens, with strong invasiveness leading to vascular damage and distant dissemination (3, 4). Clinically, SPE often presents with non-specific symptoms such as fever and cough and is frequently mistaken for common pneumonia. However, delayed intervention can rapidly progress to life-threatening complications, including necrotizing pneumonia and septic shock, and is associated with high mortality (5). Therefore, early recognition and precise intervention are essential. Central venous catheters are widely used in critically ill neonates, and common complications such as catheter obstruction, local infection, and catheter-related bloodstream infection have received considerable clinical attention (6). However, catheter-associated SPE is rarely reported owing to its low incidence. Here we present a case of presumed SPE associated with PICC-related methicillin-susceptible S. aureus infection, which progressed to bilateral pulmonary abscesses in an extremely low birth weight infant, aiming to provide a clinical reference for the early identification and precise management of this rare complication. 2.Case reportA female infant delivered by cesarean section at 27 weeks and 6 days of gestation had a birth weight of 990 g (10th percentile) and Apgar scores of 5 at 1 min and 7 at 5 min. She was admitted to the neonatal intensive care unit (NICU) immediately after birth due to respiratory distress, and received nasal Continuous Positive Airway Pressure (nCPAP) and parenteral nutrition. Enteral feeding was initiated on day 1 but was poorly tolerated, presenting with vomiting and abdominal distension. An umbilical venous catheter (UVC) was placed for the first 7 days. On postnatal day 8, the UVC was removed and replaced with a peripherally inserted central catheter (PICC). Under color Doppler ultrasound guidance, the PICC was inserted via the superficial temporal and external jugular veins into the subclavian vein and subsequently into the superior vena cava, without complications (Figure 1A). After admission, the infant's respiratory status gradually improved, and oxygen delivery was stepped down from nCPAP to heated humidified nasal cannula (HHNC, FiO2 25%, flow 4 L/min), with stable oxygen saturation. On day 14 after PICC insertion (postnatal day 21), the infant developed 3-5 apneic episodes per hour with hypoxemia (SpO2 < 85%), requiring an increase in FiO2 to 40%–50%, and escalation of respiratory support from HHNC to nCPAP (PEEP 6–8 cmH2O), accompanied by lethargy, poor responsiveness, and reduced limb tone.Figure 1Imaging findings of the infant. (A) Chest x-ray (PICC day 8, postnatal day 16): Proper PICC placement. (B) Chest x-ray (PICC day 14, postnatal day 21, onset of clinical symptoms): Patchy consolidations in both lungs with thick-walled cavities. (C) C1-2-3: Contrast-enhanced chest CT(1 day after clinical onset, postnatal day 22): Bilateral pneumonia with lung abscess formation (C-1: coronal view; C-2 and C-3: axial views at different levels). (D) Chest x-ray (treated with 4 days vancomycin and 1 day linezolid, postnatal day26): Slight progression of the right-sided lesion. (E) Chest x-ray (1week after drug discontinuation, postnatal day 67): Significant absorption of lung lesions and reduction in cavity size. (F) Chest x-ray (2 months after treatment discontinuation): No obvious abnormalities.Panel A shows a pediatric chest X-ray with an arrow indicating increased opacity along the mediastinum. Panel B displays an X-ray with arrows highlighting abnormal densities in the lower right lung. Panel C-1 is a coronal CT scan with arrows pointing to bilateral lung lesions. Panel C-2 and C-3 are axial CT scans with arrows identifying round lesions in both lungs. Panel D presents a chest X-ray with bilateral opacities marked by arrows. Panel E shows a chest X-ray with a mediastinal opacity indicated. Panel F features a chest X-ray demonstrating subtle parenchymal changes marked by an arrow.Chest x-ray revealed bilateral diffuse patchy consolidations with thick-walled cavities and surrounding exudative changes, suggestive of bilateral pulmonary abscesses. Contrast-enhanced chest CT showed: 1 multiple bilateral thick-walled cavitary lesions, with the largest measuring approximately 14.7 mm × 10.2 mm in the right lung and 20.3 mm × 12.1 mm in the left lung, with slightly irregular inner walls and patchy peripheral exudative opacities (Figure 1); 2 a well-defined, round nodule (approximately 3 mm) in the periphery of the right lung without significant contrast enhancement; 3 dense consolidation in both lower lobes with thickened and distorted pulmonary markings; and 4 localized emphysema in the left lower lobe. Laboratory parameters showed a peripheral leukocyte count was 21.11 × 109/L (reference range: 5.0–20.0 × 109/L), with neutrophils count was 15.54 × 109/L (reference range: 2.0–10.0 × 109/L); platelet count was 299 × 109/L (reference: 242–378 × 109/L); C-reactive protein (CRP) was 4.3 mg/L (reference: 0–3 mg/L). Serum 1,3-β D-glucan (G-test), galactomannan (GM-test), T-SPOT, TB assay, and nucleic acid testing for respiratory syncytial virus, adenovirus, influenza virus, and parainfluenza virus were all negative. Ultrasound of the heart and the vessels showed no obvious vegetation or thrombus formation. To exclude central nervous system involvement, a lumbar puncture was performed on postnatal day 21 prior to antibiotic administration. CSF analysis showed normal cell count and differential, protein, chloride, glucose, and negative bacterial culture, effectively ruling out meningitis.Microbiological Findings including: 1 Peripheral blood culture: 2 consecutive samples were negative; 2 PICC tip and deep sputum cultures: methicillin-susceptible S. aureus (MSSA) was isolated; 3 Next-generation sequencing (NGS): using the Illumina NovaSeq 6,000 platform. Samples (peripheral blood, PICC intraluminal blood, and deep sputum) were collected at the onset of clinical deterioration (PICC day 14, postnatal day 21), before the initiation of antibiotic therapy. Deep sputum specimens were obtained by passing a sterile suction catheter through the nasal cavity into the lower airway under aseptic conditions, with suction applied only after the catheter had bypassed the oropharynx to minimize upper-airway contamination. The procedure was performed by experienced neonatal nurse. Each sequencing run included sterile water as a negative control, and no microbial reads were detected in these controls. The validated detection threshold for a positive call was defined as ≥5 specific reads mapping to a given pathogen at the genus or species level, with a relative abundance of ≥0.5% after stringent host-background subtraction (removal of human reads). This threshold was established and validated by the performing laboratory through serial dilution experiments using reference strains (including S. aureus, E. coli, and C. albicans) spiked into negative clinical matrices at varying concentrations to determine the limit of detection, following the general principles outlined in the expert consensus on the clinical application of metagenomic next-generation sequencing for pathogen detection (7). full_text: IntroductionPost-pandemic re-emergence of Mycoplasma pneumoniae has raised concern about pediatric hospital burden and intensive-care demand. We described temporal trends, age-stratified diagnosis-coded phenotypes, pathogen-related coded co-diagnoses, and variables associated with PICU-associated hospitalization.MethodsWe conducted a single-center retrospective study based on diagnosis-coded discharge records from a tertiary maternal and child health hospital in Hubei, China. Hospitalization records of children aged 29 days to <18 years with finalized diagnosis-coded M. pneumoniae-associated illness from June 2020 to March 2026 were screened; neonatal, adult, and manually verified repeated records were excluded. A stratified chart-validation subset (n = 762) summarized microbiological evidence and selected coding-derived variables.ResultsThe analytic dataset included 33,047 pediatric hospitalization records; 16,848 (51.0%) were male and 872 (2.6%) were PICU-associated. Monthly records peaked in November 2023 (2,282), whereas PICU-associated records and rate peaked in October 2023 (99; 4.95%). Respiratory failure/hypoxemia was recorded in 6.6% of the 1–<12 mo group versus 1.3% of the 72–<144 mo group; coded sepsis/septicemia in 11.2% versus 5.9%; and cardiac abnormality/coded myocardial involvement in 25.0% versus 15.6%. Atelectasis and consolidation peaked in the 72–<144 mo group (24.1 and 13.0%). The most common pathogen-related coded co-diagnoses were respiratory syncytial virus (2,096; 6.3%), rhinovirus (2,031; 6.1%), Haemophilus influenzae (1,351; 4.1%), adenovirus (1,348; 4.1%), and influenza virus (956; 2.9%). In the extended exploratory model, age 1–<12 mo (aOR, 2.59; 95% CI, 2.07–3.24), age 12–<36 mo (aOR, 1.70; 95% CI, 1.40–2.07), influenza virus (aOR, 2.07; 95% CI, 1.50–2.86), respiratory syncytial virus (aOR, 1.83; 95% CI, 1.43–2.35), and major chronic/congenital comorbidity (aOR, 8.07; 95% CI, 6.69–9.74) were associated with PICU-associated hospitalization.ConclusionDiagnosis-coded pediatric M. pneumoniae-associated hospitalization records increased after June 2023 and peaked in November 2023, with age-structured coded phenotype patterns and measurable PICU-associated burden. Findings represent hospital-based diagnosis-coded patterns, not laboratory-adjudicated incident infections or population incidence. 2Methods2.1Study design and data sourceThis retrospective discharge-abstract study used a de-identified structured inpatient discharge dataset from Maternal and Child Health Hospital of Hubei Province. The dataset reflected routine hospital documentation, discharge diagnosis coding, and department-field recording. Because the primary analysis used finalized discharge abstracts rather than full clinical-chart adjudication, all phenotype and pathogen variables derived from discharge diagnosis labels were interpreted as diagnosis-coded variables. Reporting was guided by principles for observational studies using routinely collected health data, including transparency of data source, coding algorithms, and outcome definitions (13–15).2.2Study population and data cleaningThe initial screening dataset contained 34,562 diagnosis-coded M. pneumoniae-associated hospitalization records. Records from children aged <29 days (n = 55), records from patients aged ≥18 years (n = 1,436), and repeated hospitalization records identified through manual verification (n = 24) were excluded. The final analytic dataset included 33,047 eligible pediatric hospitalization records aged ≥29 days and <18 years (Supplementary Figure S1). The unit of analysis was the hospitalization record. Age was calculated at admission and expressed in month-based clinical categories: 1–<12 mo, 12–<36 mo, 36–<72 mo, 72–<144 mo, and 144–<216 mo. The 1–<12 mo group began at age 29 days because neonatal records had been excluded.2.3Microbiological and diagnosis-coded case definitionIn routine institutional practice, M. pneumoniae-associated illness was diagnosed by treating clinicians based on compatible clinical manifestations, radiologic findings when available, and supportive laboratory evidence, including serological evidence or pathogen detection in respiratory specimens. Laboratory evidence included serology and, when available, molecular detection by polymerase chain reaction (PCR), nucleic acid amplification testing (NAAT), targeted next-generation sequencing (tNGS), or metagenomic next-generation sequencing (mNGS). This approach was consistent with pediatric guideline recommendations and current laboratory guidance supporting the combined use of clinical features and microbiological evidence, while recognizing that NAAT-based methods provide more specific diagnostic support than single-serology evidence (2, 16). In the full discharge-abstract cohort, however, records were identified from finalized diagnosis-coded discharge records rather than full laboratory adjudication. Therefore, the analytic cohort was defined as diagnosis-coded M. pneumoniae-associated hospitalization records, not laboratory-adjudicated incident M. pneumoniae infections.2.4Pathogen-related coded co-diagnosesPathogen-related coded co-diagnoses were derived from specific pathogen-related discharge diagnosis labels. For each pathogen group, a hospitalization record was counted once if one or more corresponding pathogen-specific diagnosis labels were present; repeated labels within the same hospitalization record were not counted more than once. Non-specific infection labels such as bacterial infection, viral infection, infectious fever, respiratory tract infection, and pulmonary infection were not included in the any-pathogen summary variable. Pertussis-like syndrome and parapertussis were not counted as pertussis. Original source-language diagnosis strings are provided for reproducibility.2.5Diagnosis-coded phenotype groups and PICU-associated hospitalizationSelected pulmonary complication, extrapulmonary, severe-care, and hematologic phenotype groups were derived from discharge diagnosis labels according to predefined grouping rules (Supplementary Table S1). Each hospitalization record was counted once for a phenotype group if one or more corresponding discharge diagnosis labels were present; repeated labels within the same hospitalization record were not counted more than once. These grouped variables were defined and interpreted as diagnosis-coded phenotype groups rather than clinically adjudicated organ involvement directly attributable to M. pneumoniae. For example, cardiac abnormality/coded myocardial involvement included discharge labels such as myocardial injury, myocarditis, abnormal myocardial enzyme profile, or electrocardiographic abnormality, whereas neurologic/central nervous system (CNS)-related diagnoses included neurologic or seizure-related discharge labels. The original source-language diagnosis strings and grouping rules are provided in Supplementary Table S1 for reproducibility.PICU-associated hospitalization was defined as any hospitalization record indicating that the child received pediatric intensive care at any time during the hospital stay, based on the structured PICU field and/or department information. This definition included both direct PICU care at hospital presentation and transfer to PICU after admission to another ward. Therefore, the outcome reflects hospitalization involving PICU care rather than direct admission to the PICU at hospital presentation only.2.6Stratified chart-validation subsetTo evaluate the plausibility and supporting documentation of key discharge-coded variables, we conducted a stratified systematic chart-validation substudy of 762 records. Records were stratified by admission year and PICU-associated status; within each stratum, eligible records were ordered by admission date and selected at approximately regular intervals to improve temporal coverage. The validation subset included 247 PICU-associated records and 515 non-PICU records, intentionally enriching PICU-associated records to better assess coding-derived variables related to intensive-care-associated hospitalization. The validation extraction summarized microbiological evidence for M. pneumoniae, chart-level support for selected coded phenotype and comorbidity variables, documentation of other respiratory pathogen testing, and PICU-associated care reasons among PICU-associated validation records. Because PICU-associated records were intentionally enriched, chart-validation findings were interpreted as validation summaries rather than unweighted full-cohort prevalence estimates.2.7Statistical analysisCategorical variables were summarized as counts and percentages, and continuous variables were summarized as medians with interquartile ranges (IQRs). Age-group comparisons were performed using chi-square tests for categorical variables and Kruskal–Wallis tests for continuous variables. Because of the large sample size and multiple descriptive comparisons, p values were interpreted as exploratory, and interpretation emphasized absolute age-stratified differences rather than statistical significance alone. Monthly hospitalization counts, monthly PICU-associated records, and monthly PICU-associated rates were calculated descriptively.Logistic regression models were used to estimate adjusted odds ratios (aORs) and 95% confidence intervals (CIs) for PICU-associated hospitalization. The parsimonious model included age group, sex, and selected common pathogen-related coded co-diagnoses, including rhinovirus, Haemophilus influenzae, adenovirus, respiratory syncytial virus, and influenza virus. The extended exploratory model additionally adjusted for major chronic/congenital comorbidity, admission year, and season as categorical covariates. Season was assigned according to admission month: spring (March–May), summer (June–August), autumn (September–November), and winter (December–February). The reference categories in the extended model were 72–<144 mo for age group, 2024 for admission year, and autumn for season. Full model estimates and model summaries were reported with the model results. The models were intended to explore associations based on available coded variables rather than identify causal risk factors or construct a definitive clinical prediction model.All statistical tests were two-sided. Analyses were performed in Python version 3.11.2 using pandas, NumPy, SciPy, and statsmodels; figures were generated using Matplotlib. 2.1Study design and data sourceThis retrospective discharge-abstract study used a de-identified structured inpatient discharge dataset from Maternal and Child Health Hospital of Hubei Province. The dataset reflected routine hospital documentation, discharge diagnosis coding, and department-field recording. Because the primary analysis used finalized discharge abstracts rather than full clinical-chart adjudication, all phenotype and pathogen variables derived from discharge diagnosis labels were interpreted as diagnosis-coded variables. Reporting was guided by principles for observational studies using routinely collected health data, including transparency of data source, coding algorithms, and outcome definitions (13–15). 3Results3.1Study populationThe final analytic dataset included 33,047 pediatric diagnosis-coded M. pneumoniae-associated hospitalization records. There were 2,882 records in the 1–<12 mo group, 7,824 in the 12–<36 mo group, 10,747 in the 36–<72 mo group, 10,966 in the 72–<144 mo group, and 628 in the 144–<216 mo group. Overall, 16,848 records (51.0%) were from male patients, 872 (2.6%) were PICU-associated, and 4,100 (12.4%) had a hospital stay longer than 7 days. The median age at admission was 52.7 months (IQR, 26.5–84.8), and the median length of stay was 5 days (IQR, 4–6). full_text_sections.abstract: IntroductionPost-pandemic re-emergence of Mycoplasma pneumoniae has raised concern about pediatric hospital burden and intensive-care demand. We described temporal trends, age-stratified diagnosis-coded phenotypes, pathogen-related coded co-diagnoses, and variables associated with PICU-associated hospitalization.MethodsWe conducted a single-center retrospective study based on diagnosis-coded discharge records from a tertiary maternal and child health hospital in Hubei, China. Hospitalization records of children aged 29 days to <18 years with finalized diagnosis-coded M. pneumoniae-associated illness from June 2020 to March 2026 were screened; neonatal, adult, and manually verified repeated records were excluded. A stratified chart-validation subset (n = 762) summarized microbiological evidence and selected coding-derived variables.ResultsThe analytic dataset included 33,047 pediatric hospitalization records; 16,848 (51.0%) were male and 872 (2.6%) were PICU-associated. Monthly records peaked in November 2023 (2,282), whereas PICU-associated records and rate peaked in October 2023 (99; 4.95%). Respiratory failure/hypoxemia was recorded in 6.6% of the 1–<12 mo group versus 1.3% of the 72–<144 mo group; coded sepsis/septicemia in 11.2% versus 5.9%; and cardiac abnormality/coded myocardial involvement in 25.0% versus 15.6%. Atelectasis and consolidation peaked in the 72–<144 mo group (24.1 and 13.0%). The most common pathogen-related coded co-diagnoses were respiratory syncytial virus (2,096; 6.3%), rhinovirus (2,031; 6.1%), Haemophilus influenzae (1,351; 4.1%), adenovirus (1,348; 4.1%), and influenza virus (956; 2.9%). In the extended exploratory model, age 1–<12 mo (aOR, 2.59; 95% CI, 2.07–3.24), age 12–<36 mo (aOR, 1.70; 95% CI, 1.40–2.07), influenza virus (aOR, 2.07; 95% CI, 1.50–2.86), respiratory syncytial virus (aOR, 1.83; 95% CI, 1.43–2.35), and major chronic/congenital comorbidity (aOR, 8.07; 95% CI, 6.69–9.74) were associated with PICU-associated hospitalization.ConclusionDiagnosis-coded pediatric M. pneumoniae-associated hospitalization records increased after June 2023 and peaked in November 2023, with age-structured coded phenotype patterns and measurable PICU-associated burden. Findings represent hospital-based diagnosis-coded patterns, not laboratory-adjudicated incident infections or population incidence.
full_text_sections.methods: 2Methods2.1Study design and data sourceThis retrospective discharge-abstract study used a de-identified structured inpatient discharge dataset from Maternal and Child Health Hospital of Hubei Province. The dataset reflected routine hospital documentation, discharge diagnosis coding, and department-field recording. Because the primary analysis used finalized discharge abstracts rather than full clinical-chart adjudication, all phenotype and pathogen variables derived from discharge diagnosis labels were interpreted as diagnosis-coded variables. Reporting was guided by principles for observational studies using routinely collected health data, including transparency of data source, coding algorithms, and outcome definitions (13–15).2.2Study population and data cleaningThe initial screening dataset contained 34,562 diagnosis-coded M. pneumoniae-associated hospitalization records. Records from children aged <29 days (n = 55), records from patients aged ≥18 years (n = 1,436), and repeated hospitalization records identified through manual verification (n = 24) were excluded. The final analytic dataset included 33,047 eligible pediatric hospitalization records aged ≥29 days and <18 years (Supplementary Figure S1). The unit of analysis was the hospitalization record. Age was calculated at admission and expressed in month-based clinical categories: 1–<12 mo, 12–<36 mo, 36–<72 mo, 72–<144 mo, and 144–<216 mo. The 1–<12 mo group began at age 29 days because neonatal records had been excluded.2.3Microbiological and diagnosis-coded case definitionIn routine institutional practice, M. pneumoniae-associated illness was diagnosed by treating clinicians based on compatible clinical manifestations, radiologic findings when available, and supportive laboratory evidence, including serological evidence or pathogen detection in respiratory specimens. Laboratory evidence included serology and, when available, molecular detection by polymerase chain reaction (PCR), nucleic acid amplification testing (NAAT), targeted next-generation sequencing (tNGS), or metagenomic next-generation sequencing (mNGS). This approach was consistent with pediatric guideline recommendations and current laboratory guidance supporting the combined use of clinical features and microbiological evidence, while recognizing that NAAT-based methods provide more specific diagnostic support than single-serology evidence (2, 16). In the full discharge-abstract cohort, however, records were identified from finalized diagnosis-coded discharge records rather than full laboratory adjudication. Therefore, the analytic cohort was defined as diagnosis-coded M. pneumoniae-associated hospitalization records, not laboratory-adjudicated incident M. pneumoniae infections.2.4Pathogen-related coded co-diagnosesPathogen-related coded co-diagnoses were derived from specific pathogen-related discharge diagnosis labels. For each pathogen group, a hospitalization record was counted once if one or more corresponding pathogen-specific diagnosis labels were present; repeated labels within the same hospitalization record were not counted more than once. Non-specific infection labels such as bacterial infection, viral infection, infectious fever, respiratory tract infection, and pulmonary infection were not included in the any-pathogen summary variable. Pertussis-like syndrome and parapertussis were not counted as pertussis. Original source-language diagnosis strings are provided for reproducibility.2.5Diagnosis-coded phenotype groups and PICU-associated hospitalizationSelected pulmonary complication, extrapulmonary, severe-care, and hematologic phenotype groups were derived from discharge diagnosis labels according to predefined grouping rules (Supplementary Table S1). Each hospitalization record was counted once for a phenotype group if one or more corresponding discharge diagnosis labels were present; repeated labels within the same hospitalization record were not counted more than once. These grouped variables were defined and interpreted as diagnosis-coded phenotype groups rather than clinically adjudicated organ involvement directly attributable to M. pneumoniae. For example, cardiac abnormality/coded myocardial involvement included discharge labels such as myocardial injury, myocarditis, abnormal myocardial enzyme profile, or electrocardiographic abnormality, whereas neurologic/central nervous system (CNS)-related diagnoses included neurologic or seizure-related discharge labels. The original source-language diagnosis strings and grouping rules are provided in Supplementary Table S1 for reproducibility.PICU-associated hospitalization was defined as any hospitalization record indicating that the child received pediatric intensive care at any time during the hospital stay, based on the structured PICU field and/or department information. This definition included both direct PICU care at hospital presentation and transfer to PICU after admission to another ward. Therefore, the outcome reflects hospitalization involving PICU care rather than direct admission to the PICU at hospital presentation only.2.6Stratified chart-validation subsetTo evaluate the plausibility and supporting documentation of key discharge-coded variables, we conducted a stratified systematic chart-validation substudy of 762 records. Records were stratified by admission year and PICU-associated status; within each stratum, eligible records were ordered by admission date and selected at approximately regular intervals to improve temporal coverage. The validation subset included 247 PICU-associated records and 515 non-PICU records, intentionally enriching PICU-associated records to better assess coding-derived variables related to intensive-care-associated hospitalization. The validation extraction summarized microbiological evidence for M. pneumoniae, chart-level support for selected coded phenotype and comorbidity variables, documentation of other respiratory pathogen testing, and PICU-associated care reasons among PICU-associated validation records. Because PICU-associated records were intentionally enriched, chart-validation findings were interpreted as validation summaries rather than unweighted full-cohort prevalence estimates.2.7Statistical analysisCategorical variables were summarized as counts and percentages, and continuous variables were summarized as medians with interquartile ranges (IQRs). Age-group comparisons were performed using chi-square tests for categorical variables and Kruskal–Wallis tests for continuous variables. Because of the large sample size and multiple descriptive comparisons, p values were interpreted as exploratory, and interpretation emphasized absolute age-stratified differences rather than statistical significance alone. Monthly hospitalization counts, monthly PICU-associated records, and monthly PICU-associated rates were calculated descriptively.Logistic regression models were used to estimate adjusted odds ratios (aORs) and 95% confidence intervals (CIs) for PICU-associated hospitalization. The parsimonious model included age group, sex, and selected common pathogen-related coded co-diagnoses, including rhinovirus, Haemophilus influenzae, adenovirus, respiratory syncytial virus, and influenza virus. The extended exploratory model additionally adjusted for major chronic/congenital comorbidity, admission year, and season as categorical covariates. Season was assigned according to admission month: spring (March–May), summer (June–August), autumn (September–November), and winter (December–February). The reference categories in the extended model were 72–<144 mo for age group, 2024 for admission year, and autumn for season. Full model estimates and model summaries were reported with the model results. The models were intended to explore associations based on available coded variables rather than identify causal risk factors or construct a definitive clinical prediction model.All statistical tests were two-sided. full_text_sections.discussion: 4DiscussionThis single-center discharge-abstract study identified three major findings. First, diagnosis-coded pediatric M. pneumoniae-associated hospitalization records increased markedly from June 2023 onward, with the highest monthly total observed in November 2023, and the highest monthly PICU-associated burden preceded the peak in total monthly records. Second, age structured the distribution of coded phenotypes: younger children had higher proportions of severe-care and systemic labels, whereas school-aged children had higher proportions of structural pulmonary complication labels. Third, selected pathogen-related coded co-diagnoses and major chronic/congenital comorbidity were associated with PICU-associated hospitalization in an exploratory model.This study adds a hospital-service perspective based on routinely collected discharge abstracts to the literature on pediatric M. pneumoniae re-emergence. Clinically adjudicated cohorts are essential for defining laboratory-confirmed infection, imaging severity, treatment, and individual outcomes. In contrast, our study used a large single-center discharge-abstract dataset to describe monthly diagnosis-coded hospitalization records, age-stratified coding-derived phenotype patterns, pathogen-related coded co-diagnoses, and PICU-associated care. Thus, the principal contribution is not to estimate population incidence, prove acute infection in every record, or attribute organ involvement causally to M. pneumoniae, but to show how diagnosis-coded hospitalizations and severe-care demand were distributed over time and across age groups within a consistent tertiary pediatric service system during the post-pandemic period.The temporal pattern is consistent with international reports of delayed post-pandemic re-emergence of M. pneumoniae, including recent hospital-based pediatric data and surveillance reports (5–8, 17). A recent Italian pediatric tertiary-center study of laboratory-confirmed M. pneumoniae infection from 2017 to 2024 reported a marked post-pandemic increase in MP-related hospitalizations, whereas respiratory support requirements, PICU-related outcomes, and length of stay remained broadly comparable with the pre-pandemic period (7). That clinically adjudicated cohort provides an important clinical reference for interpreting post-pandemic hospital burden, but it differs from the present study in data structure and inference: the Italian study evaluated microbiologically confirmed infection episodes with clinical, laboratory, and radiologic information, whereas our study describes diagnosis-coded hospitalization records and hospital-service burden in a large discharge-abstract dataset. Therefore, our findings complement rather than replicate clinically adjudicated MP cohorts. They should be interpreted as hospital-based diagnosis-coded patterns rather than population incidence or laboratory-confirmed infection incidence. The Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) also notes that M. pneumoniae infection is not nationally notifiable and that surveillance relies on syndromic, laboratory, outbreak, and special-study data sources (17), further supporting a cautious interpretation of our hospital-based temporal pattern.The age-stratified phenotype pattern should be interpreted as a diagnosis-coded pattern rather than a directly adjudicated biological phenotype. The grouped variables were derived from discharge diagnosis labels and may reflect clinical disease, testing intensity, age-related documentation, clinical coding terms, and referral pathways. This concern is particularly relevant for cardiac abnormality/coded myocardial involvement, neurologic/CNS-related diagnoses, and coded sepsis/septicemia, because these categories included broad discharge-diagnosis labels rather than standardized adjudication of organ involvement. Nevertheless, the observed age-structured distribution remains clinically informative when interpreted within these boundaries. Younger children may have lower respiratory reserve and different thresholds for systemic diagnostic labeling or escalation of care, whereas school-aged children with M. pneumoniae-associated pneumonia may more often show structural pulmonary complication labels such as atelectasis and consolidation. Prior pediatric studies have described severe or refractory M. pneumoniae pneumonia, immune activation, mucus plug formation, macrolide-resistant infection, and cardiac or other extrapulmonary manifestations, supporting the biological plausibility of age-related heterogeneity while also emphasizing the need for standardized clinical, imaging, biomarker, and microbiological definitions in future studies (18–22). In line with reporting principles for studies using routinely collected health data, we therefore emphasized transparent coding rules, source-language diagnosis strings, and cautious interpretation of coding-derived variables (13–15).The pathogen-related co-diagnosis findings require careful distinction between coded co-diagnosis, laboratory co-detection, and true causative coinfection. In the full cohort, we analyzed discharge diagnosis labels rather than systematic laboratory co-detection across all children. In the chart-validation subset, microbiological evidence was summarized at the record level; however, even molecular detection may reflect asymptomatic carriage, prolonged detection, timing of sampling, or detection of a pathogen that was not the primary driver of severity (7, 23). This distinction is particularly important for RSV and influenza virus, because both pathogens can independently cause severe pediatric respiratory disease (9, 10). Recent pediatric studies have shown that respiratory virus or adenovirus co-detection in M. pneumoniae pneumonia may be clinically relevant, but co-detection alone does not establish etiologic causality, infection timing, pathogen burden, or directionality of severity (12, 24–27). Accordingly, the associations between pathogen-related coded co-diagnoses and PICU-associated hospitalization in our dataset should be interpreted as discharge-coded risk signals rather than evidence of causal coinfection.The multivariable findings are best interpreted as exploratory associations based on available coded variables rather than independent causal predictors or a definitive clinical prognostic model. Although the extended model adjusted for age, sex, selected pathogen-related coded co-diagnoses, major chronic/congenital comorbidity, admission year, and season, the full cohort did not contain standardized radiologic severity scores, inflammatory biomarkers, oxygen requirement before PICU transfer, treatment intensity, macrolide-resistance results, or pathogen load. These factors have been evaluated in clinically adjudicated pediatric M. pneumoniae studies and may influence severity, structural pulmonary complications, extrapulmonary involvement, or treatment response (18–22). Therefore, the model should not be used to infer that RSV, influenza virus, or comorbidity causally determined PICU-associated hospitalization. Rather, it should be viewed as a discharge-coded risk-stratification analysis showing which routinely available demographic, comorbidity, calendar-time, and pathogen-coded variables were associated with PICU-associated care in this hospital-based dataset.Several limitations should be considered. First, this was a single-center study conducted in a tertiary maternal and child health hospital and provincial children’s infectious disease center, and the findings may not be generalizable to community hospitals or population-level surveillance settings. Second, the primary dataset was based on structured discharge abstracts; therefore, diagnosis-coded phenotype groups may be influenced by clinical documentation, testing intensity, coding conventions, and referral pathways. full_text_sections.conclusion: 5ConclusionIn this large single-center discharge-abstract cohort, diagnosis-coded pediatric M. pneumoniae-associated hospitalization records rose above the 2020–2022 monthly range from June 2023 and peaked in November 2023, with age-structured diagnosis-coded phenotype patterns and measurable PICU-associated burden. The findings may inform hospital-based monitoring systems that consider age structure, coding-derived phenotype patterns, pathogen-related coded co-diagnoses, and intensive-care resource use. They should be interpreted as diagnosis-coded hospital-service patterns rather than laboratory-adjudicated incident infections or population incidence.
