full_text_sections.conclusion: 5ConclusionAcross 36 months of post-pandemic surveillance in Tianjin (2,597 confirmed cases), HRV, ADV and RSV were the leading viral causes of pediatric LRTI, and each of the six viruses carried a distinctive age, sex, seasonal and specimen-type profile. In a unified model adjusting simultaneously for seasonality and secular trend, RSV and HMPV, rather than IFV, showed the clearest evidence of an independent, non-seasonal climate association, whereas IFV’s prominent unadjusted climate signal proved to reflect its strong intrinsic seasonality. HBoV showed a singular July epidemic at odds with the December convergence of the other viruses, together providing a preliminary basis for pathogen-tailored early warning and prevention in northern Chinese megacities. Co-infection occurred in 4.5% of positives, centered on HRV-containing combinations whose clinical severity remains to be defined. Set alongside pre-pandemic Chinese pediatric surveillance, these findings are broadly consistent with a post-pandemic pattern of intensified, temporally compressed winter transmission, while HBoV’s summer epidemic appears to be a locally distinctive feature warranting further study. If confirmed with higher-resolution, denominator-based data, these findings could inform a hospital-level operational calendar anchored on the December peak and the secondary July HBoV peak, climate-informed early warning tailored to each pathogen’s actual (seasonally adjusted) climate sensitivity, and a refined strategy for vaccination, RSV passive immunization and infection control. Such confirmation will require multi-center cohorts, denominator-based positivity metrics, weekly- or daily-resolution meteorology, and direct pre- versus post-pandemic comparison.
full_text_sections.other: 1IntroductionLower respiratory tract infections (LRTIs)—comprising pneumonia, bronchiolitis, and related lower-airway syndromes—remain leading causes of pediatric hospitalization and mortality in children under five worldwide, with viruses accounting for the overwhelming majority of cases (Nair et al., 2010; Mulholland, 2003; Li et al., 2022). In contrast to generally self-limiting upper respiratory infections, viral LRTIs account disproportionately for admissions requiring supplemental oxygen and intensive care; moreover, certain pathogens, notably RSV and HRV, are implicated in long-term sequelae including recurrent wheeze and asthma (Li et al., 2022; Bizot et al., 2021; Royston and Tapparel, 2016). In China, the burden is amplified by dense urban populations, overlapping pathogen circulation, and the high contact rates among school-aged children, all of which sustain substantial LRTI-related hospitalizations (Cui et al., 2024; Liu et al., 2025). Following the lifting of pandemic-era non-pharmaceutical interventions, several Chinese regions reported atypical, out-of-season resurgences of RSV, Mycoplasma pneumoniae, and ADV (Del Riccio et al., 2024; Liu et al., 2025). These have been attributed both to an immunity gap accumulated during 2020–2022 and to the re-establishment of pre-pandemic transmission networks (Cohen et al., 2021; Li et al., 2024). Despite this evolving landscape, most national surveillance efforts remain narrowly focused on classical pathogens (RSV, ADV, IFV) or aggregate all respiratory infections irrespective of anatomical site. Consequently, the post-pandemic, multi-pathogen epidemiology of viral LRTI specifically in children—particularly at the city level, where targeted surveillance is most actionable—remains inadequately characterized (Terliesner et al., 2022; Xia et al., 2026).Ambient weather conditions are well-established modulators of respiratory virus transmission, operating through both physical and host-defense mechanisms (Baker et al., 2019; Xu et al., 2021). Cold, dry air favors the persistence and airborne dispersal of enveloped viruses such as RSV and influenza by stabilizing the lipid envelope, slowing droplet evaporation, and impairing upper-airway mucociliary clearance (Kudo et al., 2019; Lowen et al., 2007; Lowen and Steel, 2014). Non-enveloped viruses, including ADV and HBoV, whose protein capsids tolerate a wider range of environmental stressors, tend to circulate more evenly throughout the year (Chen et al., 2014b; Lion, 2014). Importantly, climate–virus relationships are non-linear and time-delayed; exposures occurring days to weeks before case surges often exert the dominant effect, a structure that makes distributed lag non-linear models (DLNMs) particularly suitable for fine-grained inference (Bhaskaran et al., 2013; Gasparrini et al., 2010; Gasparrini, 2011). A recent post-pandemic study from Wuhan, in central China, applied daily-resolution DLNMs to seven respiratory pathogens and identified distinct lagged climate patterns—most notably, humidity drops as 1–2-week antecedents of RSV surges and wind speed as a leading correlate of influenza activity (Li et al., 2025). Because only monthly-resolution meteorological data were available for the present 2023–2025 window (Section 2.3), a full DLNM cross-basis was not identifiable with the available degrees of freedom; we therefore adapted the same distributed-lag logic into a screening framework of single-lag quasi-Poisson models spanning 0–6-month lags, cross-validated against cross-correlation functions and, in a second step, adjusted for seasonality and secular trend within a unified model (Section 2.4). This approach is best viewed as a monthly-resolution approximation to the DLNM framework rather than a full non-linear cross-basis estimation.However, few studies have systematically examined this multi-pathogen landscape in northern China, where the continental monsoon climate—characterized by cold, dry winters; hot, humid summers; and pronounced seasonal swings in temperature, humidity, and wind—differs markedly from the subtropical conditions of Wuhan and other southern cities (Chen et al., 2014a; Cui et al., 2015; Yin et al., 2023). Tianjin, a megacity of 13 million on the North China Plain, offers a particularly valuable setting to address this gap. Its local viral spectrum extends beyond the four classical agents to include three pathogens that are less consistently surveilled but contribute substantially to pediatric LRTI: HRV, HBoV, and HMPV (Feng et al., 2024; Jiang et al., 2016; Wang et al., 2022; Zhu et al., 2020). Prior work in this area has concentrated largely on southern China or on the classical pathogens (RSV, ADV, IFV), and the lagged climatic effects of the less consistently surveilled HRV, HBoV and HMPV under a temperate continental climate have not been systematically evaluated. Precisely how these three viruses, alongside the classical agents, track climatic exposures across different lag intervals in northern China therefore remains poorly characterized—a knowledge gap that has direct implications for the design of climate-informed early-warning systems in the region.To address this, we analyzed three years of post-pandemic surveillance data (January 2023 to December 2025) from a tertiary children’s hospital in Tianjin, encompassing 2,597 virologically confirmed pediatric LRTI cases caused by six respiratory viruses. Our objectives were: (i) to describe the demographic, temporal, and specimen-type distributions of each pathogen; (ii) to characterize co-infection patterns; (iii) to test pathogen-specific associations with monthly meteorological variables using Spearman correlation and season-stratified analyses; and (iv) to evaluate lagged climate effects across 0- to 6-month intervals using cross-correlation functions and a unified quasi-Poisson generalized linear model that simultaneously adjusts for seasonality and secular trends. Finally, we discuss the practical implications of our findings for climate-informed early-warning systems and pathogen-tailored preventive strategies in northern Chinese megacities. 2.2Pathogen detectionRespiratory specimens (sputum, the predominant type; bronchoalveolar lavage fluid, BALF; nasopharyngeal swabs; and oropharyngeal swabs) were collected following standardized clinical protocols, placed into viral transport medium, and transported within two hours at 2–8 °C to the clinical laboratory. Total nucleic acids were extracted on an automated platform following the manufacturer’s instructions. All specimens were tested with the same commercial targeted next-generation sequencing (tNGS) panel, which simultaneously screens for respiratory bacteria, viruses, atypical pathogens and antimicrobial-resistance markers. Library construction, ultra-multiplex amplification of pathogen-specific genomic regions and Illumina-compatible high-throughput sequencing were performed following the manufacturer’s recommended workflow, with reads aligned against a curated pathogen reference database (Li et al., 2025; Shang et al., 2025). The vendor’s reporting algorithm assigned each detected organism a clinical pathogenicity grade, from Class A (highest confidence) through lower-confidence grades. The panel was introduced during 2023 and reached full clinical implementation in the fourth quarter of that year, after which testing volume remained broadly stable through 2024 and 2025. Monthly counts of tNGS requests could not be retrieved from the laboratory information system for the whole study window, so this account of testing volume rests on the laboratory’s implementation record rather than on an auditable series of test counts, and it should be read as such.The grade is a composite call rather than a single read-count cut-off. It is generated by an integrated scoring system that combines normalized read counts (reads per million, RPM), the breadth of genome coverage achieved across the targeted regions, and spec…

elements_zh.research_question_and_background: (C) 按病原体分组的年度病例负担。分组条形图和堆叠条形图面板显示(A)六种病原体的病例数和百分比,(B)按病原体分组的样本构成,以及(C)2023年至2025年的年度病例负担。
elements_zh.methods: 使用准泊松模型估计病原体与气候的关联,该模型考虑了季节性、长期趋势和滞后气象暴露因素。结果在2,597例病毒阳性病例中,主要病原体为HRV(30.7%)、ADV(26.6%)和RSV(20.6%),随后是HBoV(12.1%)、IFV(6.0%)和HMPV(4.0%)。
elements_zh.main_results: RSV和HBoV在婴儿和幼儿中最为常见,这与气道和免疫系统的发育一致(Feng等,2024;Jiang等,2016;Li等,2022);ADV在学龄儿童中达到高峰,IFV在较大的学龄前至学龄儿童群体中达到高峰,这与学校及其他拥挤环境中的密切接触(Fang等,2025;Yu等,2021;Zhang等,2023)一致;而HMPV则表现出中间分布。
elements_zh.interpretation_and_novelty: 据我们所知,该数据集在北方中国较为独特,因为它涵盖了2023年至2025年疫情后反弹期间的六种呼吸道病毒,包括相对较少被调查的HRV、HBoV和HMPV,并且拥有完整且时间匹配的每月气象记录。4.1主要流行病学特征在六种病毒中,HRV、ADV和RSV是导致儿童LRTI的主要原因,每种病原体都有明确的流行病学特征。
elements_zh.scientific_and_public_health_significanc: 强年龄组×病原体关联进一步强调了需要建立明确的年龄分层监测框架。这六种病原体也分为两个不同的季节性群体。
elements_zh.limitations_and_evidence_strength: 4.5%的阳性病例出现了合并感染,主要集中在包含HRV的组合中,其临床严重程度仍需进一步定义。

analysis_en.research_question_and_background: (C) Annual case burden, stacked by pathogen.Grouped bar and stacked bar chart panel showing (A) case numbers and percentages for six pathogens, (B) specimen composition by pathogen, and (C) annual case burden from 2023 to 2025.
analysis_en.study_design_and_population: HRV was the most frequently detected virus (796 cases, 30.7%), followed by ADV (692, 26.6%), RSV (536, 20.6%), HBoV (313, 12.1%), IFV (155, 6.0%) and HMPV (105, 4.0%) (Figure 2A; Table 1).
analysis_en.methods: Pathogen–climate associations were estimated using a quasi-Poisson model that adjusted for seasonality, secular trend, and lagged meteorological exposures.ResultsAmong 2,597 virus-positive cases, the leading pathogens were HRV (30.7%), ADV (26.6%), and RSV (20.6%), followed by HBoV (12.1%), IFV (6.0%), and HMPV (4.0%).
analysis_en.main_results: RSV and HBoV were most prevalent in infants and toddlers, in line with airway and immune development (Feng et al., 2024; Jiang et al., 2016; Li et al., 2022); ADV peaked in school-aged children and IFV in the older preschool-to-school-age range, consistent with close-contact transmission in schools and other crowded settings (Fang et al., 2025; Yu et al., 2021; Zhang et al., 2023); and HMPV showed an intermediate distribution.
analysis_en.interpretation_and_novelty: To our knowledge, the dataset is unusual for northern China in spanning six respiratory viruses, including the comparatively under-surveyed HRV, HBoV and HMPV, over the full 2023–2025 post-pandemic rebound window, with a complete and time-matched monthly meteorological record.4.1Principal epidemiological featuresAcross the six viruses, HRV, ADV and RSV were the leading causes of pediatric LRTI, and each pathogen carried a well-defined demographic profile.
analysis_en.scientific_and_public_health_significanc: The strong age-group × pathogen association reinforces the need for an explicitly age-stratified surveillance framework.The six pathogens also fell into two distinct seasonal groups.
analysis_en.limitations_and_evidence_strength: Co-infection occurred in 4.5% of positives, centered on HRV-containing combinations whose clinical severity remains to be defined.

title_zh: 流行病学和滞后气候驱动因素对中国天津市儿童病毒性下呼吸道感染(2023–2025)的影响
source_body_en: BackgroundFollowing the lifting of pandemic-era restrictions, China experienced a sharp resurgence in pediatric respiratory infections; however, post-pandemic epidemiological and climatic data on lower respiratory tract infections (LRTIs) from the temperate continental climate of northern China remain scarce.MethodsIn this retrospective, single-center surveillance study, we characterized the post-pandemic epidemiology of six respiratory viruses in children hospitalized with LRTI in Tianjin and assessed their pathogen-specific, lagged climatic associations. 2Materials and methods2.1Study design, setting and populationWe conducted a retrospective single-center surveillance study at the Department of Respiratory Medicine, Tianjin Children’s Hospital (Ma-Chang campus), the only tertiary-A comprehensive children’s hospital in Tianjin. This last criterion operated at the level of the child rather than of the laboratory result: whenever the tNGS report carried a Class A detection of a bacterial, atypical or non-panel viral pathogen alongside one of the six target viruses, the case was removed from the cohort at eligibility screening, so no such child contributes to any analysis reported here. Children aged 0–18 years hospitalized between January 2023 and December 2025 were tested by targeted next-generation sequencing for human rhinovirus (HRV), adenovirus (ADV), respiratory syncytial virus (RSV), human bocavirus (HBoV), influenza virus (IFV), and human metapneumovirus (HMPV). Pathogen–climate associations were estimated using a quasi-Poisson model that adjusted for seasonality, secular trend, and lagged meteorological exposures.ResultsAmong 2,597 virus-positive cases, the leading pathogens were HRV (30.7%), ADV (26.6%), and RSV (20.6%), followed by HBoV (12.1%), IFV (6.0%),...
abstract_zh: 背景在解除疫情管控措施后,中国经历了儿童呼吸道感染的急剧回升;然而,关于北方中国温带大陆性气候地区疫情后下呼吸道感染(LRTIs)的流行病学和气候数据仍然稀缺。方法本项回顾性单中心监测研究旨在描述天津住院儿童中六种呼吸道病毒在疫情后的流行病学情况,并评估其与气候因素的特定病原体相关性。2材料与方法2.1研究设计、设置和人群我们在天津儿童医院(马场校区)呼吸科开展回顾性单中心监测研究,该医院是天津唯一的三级甲等综合性儿童医院。这一标准适用于儿童而非实验室结果:每当tNGS报告中检测到细菌、非典型或非检测面板病毒病原体的同时也检测到六种目标病毒之一时,该病例将在资格筛选时被排除在队列研究之外,因此此处报告的任何分析均不包含此类儿童。2023年1月至2025年12月期间住院的0至18岁儿童接受了针对人类鼻病毒(HRV)、腺病毒(ADV)、呼吸道合胞病毒(RSV)、人类博卡病毒(HBoV)、流感病毒(IFV)和人类副流感病毒(HMPV)的靶向下一代测序检测。使用准泊松模型估计病原体与气候的关联,该模型考虑了季节性、长期趋势和滞后气象暴露。结果在2597例病毒阳性病例中,主要病原体为HRV(30.7%)、ADV(26.6%)和RSV(20.6%),随后是HBoV(12.1%)、IFV(6.0%)和HMPV(4.0%)(图2A;表1)。

title: Dissecting the mechanism of action of the adjuvant system AS01 in human immune cells: synergy of QS-21 and monophosphoryl lipid A and role of type I interferons

source_records.title: Dissecting the mechanism of action of the adjuvant system AS01 in human immune cells: synergy of QS-21 and monophosphoryl lipid A and role of type I interferons

full_text: The adjuvant system AS01 comprised of the TLR4 agonist monophosphoryl lipid A (MPLA) and the saponin QS-21 embedded in liposomes is currently used in recombinant vaccines against shingles, respiratory syncytial virus infection, and malaria. The efficacy of these vaccines is attributed to the strong immunostimulatory effect of AS01. While preclinical studies have shed light on the mechanisms by which AS01 enhances immune responses, few studies have been conducted with human immune cells to dissect how the two immunostimulants work individually and in combination. We investigated the effect of AS01 on human THP-1 cells and peripheral blood mononuclear cells (PBMCs) and found that it induced secretion of a broad panel of chemokines and a modest number of cytokines. Among the chemokines, CCL3 and CCL4 were found to have the greatest fold increase. Inhibition of TLR4 signaling revealed variable dependence on TLR4, while experiments with liposomes formulated with a TLR4 agonist, QS-21, or both demonstrated synergistic effects on the induction of many chemokines and TNF. AS01 induced strong expression of interferon-stimulated genes; this was greatly reduced by treatment with an antibody that blocks the type I interferon (IFN) receptor, indicating that AS01 induced a type I IFN-associated transcriptional signature that is partially dependent on signaling via the type I IFN receptor. AS01 selectively increased the expression of CD83 on THP-1 cells and this effect was found to be mostly driven by QS-21. This work provides novel insights into the mechanisms by which AS01 stimulates human immune cells. Materials and methodsCellsHuman THP-1 cells (TIB-202; American Type Culture Collection, Manassas, VA, USA) were cultured in complete RPMI (RPMI 1640 supplemented with 2 mM L-glutamine, 55 μM 2-mercaptoethanol, 1× non-essential amino acids, 10 mM HEPES, 100 U/ml penicillin, 100 μg/ml streptomycin, and 0.25 μg/ml amphotericin) with 10% FBS (all from ThermoFisher Scientific, Waltham, MA, USA). HEK-BlueTM hTLR4 cells (Invivogen, San Diego, CA, USA) were maintained in DMEM supplemented with 2 mM L-glutamine, 100 U/ml penicillin, 100 μg/ml streptomycin, and 100 μg/ml normocin (Invivogen). THP1-Dual cells (InvivoGen) were cultured in complete RPMI supplemented with 10% FBS, 10 mg/ml blasticidin, 100 μg/ml zeocin (Invivogen), and 100 μg/ml normocin. Human peripheral blood mononuclear cells (PBMCs) pooled from five donors were purchased from HumanCells Biosciences (Milpitas, CA, USA).AdjuvantsAS01B from Zoster Vaccine Recombinant, Adjuvanted SHINGRIXTM purchased from Myonex (Horsham, PA, USA) was used in all experiments except for the liposome variants study. Liposome variants with component ratios similar to AS01 were synthesized to assess the potential synergy between the TLR4 agonist and QS-21. These LPs were formulated through a classic thin-film hydration extrusion process as described elsewhere (29) using cholesterol (Avanti Research, Alabaster, AL, USA), 1, 2-dioleoyl-sn-glycero-3-phosphocholine (DOPC; Avanti Research), phosphorylated hexaacyl disaccharide (PHAD; Avanti Research), and QS-21 (Desert King, Chula Vista, CA, USA).Cell stimulationTHP-1 cells (5 x 105 cells/mL) and PBMCs (2 x 106 cells/mL) were seeded in 96 or 24 well plates in cell growth media and incubated with the indicated dilutions of AS01, liposome variants, or LPS (from E. Coli 0111:B4; Invivogen) at 100 ng/mL. In some experiments, cells were pre-incubated with 10 μM TAK-242 (SelleckChem, Houston, TX, USA), 10 μg/mL neutralizing anti-human TLR4 antibody (clone W7C11, Invivogen) or 20 μg/mL neutralizing anti-human IFNAR1 (Invivogen). Supernatants were harvested after 24 h unless otherwise specified. Supernatants were immediately analyzed for TNF and IL-1β or frozen at -80 °C for later analysis with the 96-plex chemokine/cytokine assay. In other experiments cells were collected for flow cytometry analysis or RNA isolation. The HEK-BlueTM hTLR4 and THP-1 Dual reporter cells were cultured in 96 well plates and stimulated with 12.5% AS01. Supernatants were aspirated after 24 h and analyzed for alkaline phosphatase and luciferase activity.Cytokine concentration measurementsSupernatants were analyzed for the concentration of TNF and IL-1β by ELISA (human TNF-α DuoSet and human IL-1β/IL-1F2 DuoSet, R&D Systems, Minneapolis, MN, USA). Supernatants were analyzed for a panel of 96 chemokines, cytokines and growth factors (Human Cytokine/Chemokine 96-Plex Discovery Assay® Array (HD96), Eve Technologies, Calgary, AB, Canada). Cytokine concentrations below the minimal detection limit were given a value equal to the lowest concentration of the standards and concentrations above the maximal detection limit were given a value equal to the highest concentration of the standards.Quantitative reverse transcription-polymerase chain reactionTHP-1 cells were collected following incubation with AS01 or medium control for RNA extraction. Total RNA was extracted using the Quick-RNA Miniprep Kit (Zymo Research, Irvine, CA, USA) according to the manufacturer’s protocol. RNA concentration and purity were assessed by spectrophotometry (NanoDrop One, Thermo Scientific). Complementary DNA (cDNA) was synthesized from 0.5 μg of total RNA using the iScript Reverse Transcription Supermix kit (BioRad, Hercules, CA, USA) following the manufacturer’s instructions. Gene expression was quantified by RT-qPCR using PowerUp SYBR Green Master Mix (Thermo Fisher Scientific) on a QuantStudio 3 Real-Time PCR System (Thermo Fisher Scientific). qPCR data were analyzed using the comparative Cq (ΔΔCq) method as described by Livak and Schmittgen (30). Cq values of target genes were normalized to the geometric mean of the reference housekeeping genes ACTB (β-actin) and GAPDH (glyceraldehyde 3-phosphate dehydrogenase) to obtain ΔCq values. Relative expression levels were calculated as 2-ΔΔCq with expression in the indicated control condition set to 1.0. Primer sets used for qRT-PCR are listed in Supplementary Table 5.Western blottingFollowing stimulation with AS01 or medium only, THP-1 cells were collected and washed once with ice-cold phosphate-buffered saline (PBS). Cell pellets were lysed on ice in RIPA Lysis and Extraction Buffer (Thermo Fisher Scientific) with HaltTM Protease and Phosphatase Inhibitor Cocktail (Thermo Fisher Scientific). Lysates were incubated on ice for 10 min with intermittent mixing and purified by centrifugation at 15 000 × g for 15 min at 4 °C. The supernatants were collected and resuspended with 4× Laemmli sample buffer containing dithiothreitol (Bio-Rad) and heated at 95 °C for 5 min. Samples were separated by SDS-PAGE using 4–20% Mini-PROTEAN TGX precast gels (Bio-Rad). Proteins were then transferred onto nitrocellulose membranes using a Trans-Blot Turbo transfer system with Trans-Blot Turbo transfer packs (Bio-Rad) according to the manufacturer’s protocol. Membranes were blocked for 1 h at room temperature in SuperBlockTM Blocking Buffer (Thermo Fisher Scientific) and incubated overnight at 4 °C with primary antibodies diluted in blocking buffer. The following primary antibodies were used: phospho-STAT1 (Tyr701) (Cell Signaling Technology, Danvers, MA, USA, Cat. No. 7649), STAT1 (Cell Signaling Technology, Cat. No. 9172), phospho-STAT6 (Cell Signaling Technology, Cat. No. 9364), STAT6 (Cell Signaling Technology, Cat. No. 5397) at 1:1000 dilution and GAPDH (Cell Signaling Technology, Cat. No. 2118) at 1:2000 dilution. After primary incubation, membranes were washed three times with Tris Buffered Saline (TBS)-Tween 20 and incubated for 1 h at room temperature with HRP-conjugated anti-rabbit IgG secondary antibody (Cell Signaling Technology, Cat. No. 7074). The membranes were washed again for 3 times with TBS-Tween 20 for 10 min and subsequently developed with Clarity Max Western ECL substrate (Bio-Rad) and captured using an Syngene G:Box chemi imager (Fisher Scientific). Quantification of the western blots was performed with Image Lab 6.1 software (Bio-Rad).Flow cytometryTHP-1 cells were transferred to a 96-well round bottom tissue culture treated plate (CELLTREAT Scientific Products, Ayer, MA, USA) at 0.5 x 106 cells/mL in 200 μL cell staining buffer (BioLegend, San Diego, CA, USA). The cells were first stained with Zombie Red Fixable Viability Dye (BioLegend). To prevent nonspecific antibody binding, cells were then incubated with Human Fc Receptor Blocking Solution (BioLegend) for 10 min at room temperature prior to antibody labeling. Cells were incubated with fluorochrome-conjugated antibodies specific to various surface markers for 45 min at 4 °C in the dark. Antibodies used are listed in Supplementary Table 6. After labeling, cells were washed and fixed in 4% paraformaldehyde prior to acquisition. Data were acquired on an Attune NxT Flow Cytometer (Thermo Fisher Scientific). Compensation was performed using single-stained UltraComp eBeads (Thermo Fisher Scientific) for each fluorochrome according to the manufacturer’s instructions. Gates were defined using fluorescence minus one (FMO) controls where appropriate. The data was analyzed using FlowJo software (FlowJo, Ashland, OR, USA). Median fluorescence intensity (MFI) and percentage of positive cells were quantified.Statistical analysisThe statistical significance of differences between experimental groups was determined by one-way analysis of variance (ANOVA) test followed by a Tukey’s multiple comparisons test. The differences in mRNA expression were analyzed by converting the fold change into log10 values, followed by two-way ANOVA and Sidak’s multiple comparison test. Statistical analyses were performed with GraphPad Prism version 10.4.1 (GraphPad Software, San Diego, CA, USA) for Windows. ResultsDetermination of optimal AS01 stimulation conditionsThe adjuvant AS01 comes in two forms, AS01B containing 100 μg/mL of MPLA and 100 μg/mL QS-21, and AS01E with half those concentrations (6). We used AS01B in our studies and refer to it throughout this manuscript as AS01. Previous publications have reported a wide range of concentrations to evaluate the effect of AS01 on human immune cells ranging from a 1:100 dilution to a 1:4 dilution (i.e., 1.0 μg/mL to 25 μg/mL MPLA and QS-21) (28, 31, 32). We therefore first determined the effect of serial dilutions of AS01 on THP-1 cells using the concentration of TNF and IL-1β in 24 h supernatants as markers of cell stimulation. AS01 induced secretion of TNF in a dose-dependent manner with the highest concentration observed at 50% AS01 (Figure 1a). Incubation with AS01 also caused a dose-dependent, but very limited release of IL-1β (Figure 1b). Importantly, exposure of THP-1 cells to AS01 did not induce significant cell membrane damage as indicated by the absence of LDH release even at the highest concentration of 50% (Figure 1c). In addition to the AS01 concentration, we also evaluated the effect of the incubation time on TNF secretion induced by AS01 and 24 h yielded the maximum production (Figure 1d). Based on these data and practical considerations, we chose 24 h stimulation with 12.5% AS01 as the assay conditions.Figure 1Effect of concentration of AS01 and incubation time on THP-1 cells. (a–c) THP-1 cells were incubated for 24 h with 100 ng/mL LPS or serial dilutions of AS01 starting from 50% (contains 50 μg/mL MPLA and 50 μg/mL QS-21) and the supernatants were analyzed for TNF (a), IL-1β (b) and LDH (c). (d) Concentration of TNF in the supernatants of THP-1 cells stimulated with serial dilutions of AS01 for 6, 24 or 48 hours. Bars indicate the mean ± SD of triplicate wells. *p < 0.05; **p < 0.01; ***p < 0.001; ****p < 0.0001.Four-panel scientific bar graph illustrating cytokine and cytotoxicity assay results. Panel a shows TNF levels with LPS and various AS01 concentrations, panel b shows IL-1β levels, panel c shows LDH release, and panel d shows TNF over time. Statistical significance is indicated.AS01 induced a broad chemokine response and limited cytokine response from THP-1 cells and primary blood leukocytesUsing the optimized culture conditions, THP-1 cells were incubated with 12.5% AS01 and supernatants were evaluated by multiplex assay to measure the concentration of 30 chemokines and 66 cytokines and growth factors (full list of chemokines, cytokines and growth factors see Supplementary Table 1). AS01 significantly increased the secretion of 10 chemokines from about two-fold for CXCL12 to nearly 1, 000-fold for CCL4 compared to medium controls (Figure 2a; Supplementary Table 2). AS01 increased the secretion of six out of 66 cytokines and growth factors (Figure 2b; Supplementary Table 2) and the concentrations were relatively low with only the concentrations of IL-1RA and TNF exceeding 100 pg/ml.Figure 2Chemokine and cytokine secretion from THP-1 cells stimulated with AS01. THP-1 cells were incubated for 24 h with medium, 12.5% AS01 (12.5 μg/mL MPLA and QS-21), or LPS (100 ng/mL) and the concentrations of chemokines and cytokines were determined. The graphs show the chemokines (a) and cytokines or growth factors (b) that were significantly increased by AS01 compared with the medium control at p < 0.01 and had a concentration > 10 pg/mL in AS01 supernatants. The bars indicate the mean ± SD of triplicate wells.Bar charts compare cytokine and chemokine concentrations in cell culture supernatants for three conditions: medium, AS01, and LPS. Panel a displays CCL and CXCL family concentrations; panel b shows IL and TNF levels. LPS generally induces the highest concentrations across most factors, particularly CCL2, CCL3, CCL4, CXCL8, and TNF. AS01 induces intermediate levels, while medium consistently produces the lowest concentrations. Error bars indicate standard deviation.To confirm the ability of AS01 to induce chemokine and cytokine secretion in primary human immune cells, PBMCs pooled from five healthy donors (to avoid donor-to-donor variability) were incubated with medium, AS01, or LPS and 24 h supernatants were collected for 96-plex chemokine/cytokine analysis. While there was no measurable chemokine or cytokine production from cells incubated with media as control, there was again a robust induction of chemokines by AS01 with a significant increase (at p < 0.01) in 15 of the 30 chemokines tested (Figure 3a; Supplementary Table 3). Similar to THP-1 cells, AS01 induced increased secretion of CCL3, CCL4, CCL8, CXCL1, CXCL8 and CXCL11 by PBMCs. In addition, AS01-stimulated PBMCs secreted CCL1, CCL7, CCL13, CCL20, CCL22, CCL23, CCL28, CXCL5 and CXCL6, although the increases were modest compared with the medium control. AS01 increased secretion of 12 cytokines and growth factors (Figure 3b; Supplementary Table 3), three of which (IL-1β, IL-1RA, TNF) were also induced in THP-1 cells. There was a marked induction of the pro-inflammatory cytokines IL-1α, IL-1β, IL-6 and TNF as well as anti-inflammatory cytokines, in particular IL-1RA and IL-10.Figure 3Chemokine and cytokine secretion by human PBMCs stimulated with AS01. Pooled PBMCs were incubated for 24 h with medium, 12.5% AS01 (12.5 μg/mL MPLA and QS-21), or LPS (100 ng/mL) and the concentrations of chemokines and cytokines were determined. The graphs show the chemokines (a) and cytokines or growth factors (b) that were significantly increased by AS01 compared with the medium control at p < 0.01 and had a concentration > 10 pg/mL in AS01 supernatants. The bars indicate the mean ± SD of triplicate wells.Two-panel grouped bar chart depicting cytokine and chemokine concentrations in picograms per milliliter measured by three treatments: medium (white), AS01 (red), and LPS (gray). Panel a shows concentrations of CCL and CXCL chemokines, while panel b presents selected interleukins, colony-stimulating factors, and TNF. LPS generally results in the highest concentrations, followed by AS01, then medium. Error bars indicate variability.AS01 engages the TLR4 receptor in THP-1 cellsTo determine the role of TLR4 signaling in the response to AS01, THP-1 cells were incubated with the TLR4-antagonist TAK-242 prior to the addition of AS01. Supernatants were then analyzed by multiplex assay for the same panel of 96 chemokines, cytokines, and growth factors. The degree of inhibition of chemokine and cytokine secretion by TAK-242 varied from 0 to 88.3% (Figure 4a). The partial inhibition of TNF secretion by interference of TLR4 signaling from TAK-242 was confirmed with an anti-TLR4 antibody (Figure 4b). These experiments indicate a role for TLR4 signaling in the immunostimulatory activity of AS01. To further validate these findings, the effect of AS01on reporter cell lines was determined. AS01 activated a human TLR4 reporter cell line (HEK-BlueTM hTLR4) and activated both NF-κB and Interferon Regulatory Factor (IRF) signaling pathways in THP-1 dual reporter cells, although at a much lower level than LPS (Figures 4d–f).Figure 4Role of TLR4 signaling in AS01-induced chemokine and cytokine secretion by THP-1 cells. (a) Effect of the TLR4-inhibitor TAK-242 on the secretion of chemokines and cytokines. (b) Effect of the TLR4 inhibitor TAK-242 and an anti-TLR4 antibody on TNF secretion by THP-1 cells. (c) Effect of priming of THP-1 cells with LPS on AS01-induced IL-1β release into the supernatant. (d) TLR4 signaling induced by AS01 and LPS in a human TLR4 HEK-BlueTM reporter cell line. (e, f) Activation of NF-κB (e) and IRF (f) signaling pathways induced by AS01 and LPS in THP-1 DualTM cells. Bars indicate the mean ± SD of three to six replicate wells. *p < 0.05; **p < 0.01; ***p < 0.001; ****p < 0.0001; ns, not significant.Six-panel scientific figure with bar graphs and statistical annotations. Panel a shows horizontal bars for cytokines and chemokines with percent inhibition by TAK-242; CXCL10 is most inhibited. Panels b and c show vertical bar graphs of TNF and IL-1β concentrations, with significant differences between conditions annotated by asterisks. Panels d, e, and f show TLR4, NF-κB, and…

full_text_sections.discussion: DiscussionThe AS01 adjuvant was developed to utilize the potential synergy between two known immunostimulators, MPLA and QS-21, delivered together to antigen-presenting cells in the form of LPs (6, 35). Preclinical studies have demonstrated synergistic effects of QS-21 and MPLA in enhancing CD4+ and CD8+ T cell responses, albeit with a stronger role for QS-21 than MPLA (20, 36). There was no difference in serum antibody titers between mice immunized with LP-QS-21 versus AS01 or AS01-like formulations (20, 36, 37). Cell culture experiments with human cells revealed synergistic effects of QS-21 and PHAD on the secretion of certain cytokines and the activation of CD8+ T cells (37). Our results support synergistic roles of QS-21 and MPLA in the induction of cytokine secretion by THP-1 cells and further demonstrate that the contribution of each component varied and was cytokine-dependent.Monocytes respond to immunopotentiators by the secretion of chemokines and cytokines that in turn recruit and activate other immune cells resulting in inflammation and initiation of the adaptive immune response. The NF-κB and IRF signaling pathways are two major signaling pathways involved in the transcription of chemokine and cytokine genes. AS01 induced activation of both pathways as indicated by the experiments with THP-1 Dual cells and this is also reflected in the robust secretion of a broad panel of chemokines and a more modest number of cytokines. The strong induction of chemokine secretion is consistent with the rapid accumulation of neutrophils, monocytes and dendritic cells at the injection site following intramuscular injection of AS01 in mice (21). These cells all participate in the uptake of vaccine antigen and transport to the draining lymph node as demonstrated in experiments with cannulated sheep (23). The NF-κB transcription factors control the production of cytokines like TNF and the chemokines CXCL1 and CXCL8 which attract neutrophils via chemokine receptors CXCR1 and CXCR2, and CCL2, CCL3, CCL4, CCL5, and CCL8 which attract lymphocytes, monocytes, macrophages and dendritic cells via chemokine receptors CCR1, CCR2, and CCR5 (38, 39). On the other hand, CXCL9, CXCL10, and CXCl11, which attract CD4+ and CD8+ T cells and NK cells via CXCR3 (38, 39) are associated with the IRF signaling pathway. Among the nine IRFs identified in human cells, IRF3 is constitutively expressed. Activation of IRF3 leads to the transcription and secretion of IFN-β which binds to the IFN receptor and induces Interferon Stimulated Genes (ISGs) via JAK-STAT signaling. One of the ISGs is IRF7 which contributes to positive feedback and amplification of the ISG expression (40, 41). In addition, a subset of ISGs can be induced directly by IRF3 without the involvement of the IFN-receptor (42, 43). It has recently been suggested that MPLA does not efficiently activate the IRF3 pathway and does not induce type I IFN in human cells (6). However, this is not consistent with the literature as both naturally derived MPLA and synthetic PHAD induce IFN-β and interferon-stimulated genes in human dendritic cells (11). We did not observe an increased concentration of type I IFNs in the supernatant of THP-1 cells or PBMCs following incubation with AS01. Similarly, AS01 did not induce an increase of IFN-α in cultures of human lymph node slices (31). Studies have shown that secreted IFNs are rapidly bound by their receptors as they act primarily in an autocrine and paracrine fashion to induce the expression of interferon-stimulated genes (ISGs) which play important roles in limiting viral replication (44, 45). Indeed, we observed increased expression of IFNB mRNA as well as the antiviral ISGs IFIH1, IFIT1, ISG15, MX1, and OAS1 in THP-1 cells stimulated with AS01. The increased expression of ISGs was inhibited by blocking the type I IFN receptor, confirming that this response is driven by AS01-induced type I IFN. Type I IFNs not only activate antiviral mechanisms as part of the innate immune response to viral infections but also enhance the adaptive immune responses. They stimulate dendritic cell maturation (46, 47), the expansion and differentiation of CD4+ and CD8+ T cells (48, 49), and the antibody response via direct and indirect effects on B cells (50, 51). On the other hand, transient inhibition of the type I IFN receptor at the time of vaccination increased the immune response to live attenuated viral vaccines and mRNA vaccines and enhanced the development of CD8+ effector and memory T cells (52–54). Together, these data suggest that induction of type I IFNs in antigen-presenting cells contributes to the immunostimulatory effect of AS01, while inhibition of type I IFN or IFN signaling at the time of vaccination may have a beneficial effect for certain vaccine applications.Previous studies in mice have revealed rapid expression of Ifng mRNA in the draining lymph node following injection of AS01 and identified NK cells and CD8+ T cells as the main cellular sources of the early IFN-γ response (20). The concentration of IFN-γ in serum of humans and nonhuman primates increased following injection of an AS01-adjuvanted vaccine (20), and the production of IFN-γ and IFN-γ-related chemokines such as CXCL9 and CXCL10 is considered a “hallmark of the AS01 innate signature” (6). Furthermore, incubation of human lymph node slices with AS01 or an AS01-like adjuvant induced increased secretion of IFN-γ (31, 55) with NK cells as the main source (55). We did not observe a significant increase of IFN-γ in supernatants of THP-1 cells or PBMCs incubated with AS01. However, AS01 increased the expression of IFNG mRNA in THP-1 cells. Although T cells and NK cells are generally considered the main sources of IFN-γ, antigen-presenting cells are another potential source of this cytokine (56). Blocking the type I IFN receptor reduced the expression of IFNG mRNA indicating that the response is induced by type I IFN as shown previously for human dendritic cells (57).The greatest fold increase in chemokine secretion in THP-1 cells and PBMCs was measured for CCL3 and CCL4, chemokines that preferentially attract CD4 and CD8 T cells (58). Previous studies have shown that PBMCs and isolated peripheral blood monocytes secrete CCL4 upon stimulation with the TLR agonists poly(I:C), LPS and R848 (59) and with the squalene emulsion adjuvant MF59 (60), but not with an aluminum hydroxide adjuvant (60). Depletion of monocytes from PBMCs abolished the secretion of CCL4 following stimulation with MF59, suggesting a negligible contribution of other cell types (60). In contrast, incubation of whole blood cultures and PBMCs with the TLR7/8 agonist R848 increased the number of CCL4+ cells as determined by intracellular cytokine staining, but the largest proportion of CCL4+ cells were neutrophils in whole blood cultures and NK cells among PBMCs rather than monocytes (61). While the level of CCL4 secretion by neutrophils and NK cells relative to monocytes was not determined, this finding suggests that cells other than monocytes can contribute to the production of CCL4 at the injection site and draining lymph node following injection of AS01 adjuvant. CCL4 was identified as a potential marker of vaccine reactogenicity in a human cell culture system of PBMCs and endothelial cells (MIMIC PTE) incubated with 10 different vaccines (62). In this study, three bacterial vaccines, but not the AS01-adjuvanted Shingrix vaccine, induced CCL4 secretion. However, the vaccines were serially diluted starting at 1:100, which is a much lower concentration of AS01 than what was used in our experiments.In our study, AS01 induced modest activation of TLR4 as indicated by the response of HEK-BlueTM hTLR4 cells and consistent with the effect on THP-1 Dual cells. As previously reported, embedding MPLA in LPs dampens its biological activity (12, 13). Similarly, the incorporation of QS-21 in LPs reduces its activity which is important to limit the reactogenicity of…
full_text_sections.other: IntroductionThe use of purified or recombinant protein antigens improves the safety and tolerability of vaccines compared to live attenuated or inactivated viral vaccines while it facilitates their formulation, production and characterization. However, such antigens are often poorly immunogenic on their own and require the addition of adjuvants, substances that enhance the immune response to vaccine antigens (1–3). Adjuvants are also used to induce a protective immune response in individuals with less responsive immune systems because of age, underlying disease or medical treatment. Furthermore, the addition of adjuvants may allow for a reduced amount of antigen in vaccines and increase the duration of protective immune responses. Adjuvants in licensed vaccines are heterogeneous in chemical and physical composition and include aluminum salts, oil-in-water emulsions, saponins and Toll-like receptor (TLR) agonists or combinations of these (4, 5). Many adjuvants were developed empirically and their mechanism of action (MoA) remains only partially understood (2, 3).The adjuvant AS01 is used in a vaccine against malaria and in vaccines that target the elderly population, namely shingles (Varicella zoster) and respiratory syncytial virus (6). The adjuvant contains the TLR4 agonist monophosphoryl lipid A (MPLA) and the saponin QS-21, formulated into liposomes (LPs) composed of dioleoyl phosphatidylcholine and cholesterol in a phosphate buffer that are approximately 106 nm in diameter (7). MPLA is prepared by sequential acid and base hydrolysis of the lipopolysaccharide (LPS) of Salmonella enterica serovar Minnesota, resulting in a complex mixture of congeners with different numbers of acyl groups (8). MPLA and LPS are both ligands of TLR4, but MPLA has reduced toxicity compared with LPS (9). Activation of TLR4 by LPS engages the adaptor molecules MyD88 and TRIF resulting in the secretion of pro-inflammatory cytokines and type I interferons, respectively. Studies in mice attributed the reduced toxicity of MPLA to a decreased ability to signal via MyD88 resulting in lower production of inflammatory cytokines without affecting the ability to enhance the adaptive immune response (10). However, there are marked species-specific differences in TLR4 signaling as certain MPLA congeners are inhibitory for human TLR4, but not mouse TLR4, resulting in an overall lower response of human TLR4 to MPLA (8, 11). This should be kept in mind when evaluating the response of human cells to AS01 containing naturally derived MPLA as opposed to formulations containing a synthetic form of MPLA such as phosphorylated hexaacylated disaccharide (PHAD) (11). Incorporation of MPLA in LPs as is the case in AS01 further reduces its reactogenicity (12, 13). QS-21 is a saponin isolated from the bark of the South American soapbark tree, Quillaja saponaria (14). Although QS-21 has lower toxicity than other saponin fractions, it still has hemolytic activity, limiting its direct use as a vaccine adjuvant. The hemolytic activity is caused by the high affinity of QS-21 for cholesterol leading to disruption of cell membranes. This high affinity to cholesterol, however, also allows its incorporation in cholesterol-containing LPs which eliminates the toxicity and stabilizes QS-21 (15). QS-21, which is taken up by cells via cholesterol-dependent endocytosis, stimulates both antibody and cell-mediated immune responses when administered in vaccine formulations. QS-21 alone or incorporated in LPs stimulates the release of IL-1β from human peripheral blood mononuclear cells (PBMCs), mouse macrophages, and dendritic cells primed with TLR4 agonists in vitro (16–18). Destabilization of lysosomes results in the release of cathepsin B, phosphorylation of Syk, and activation of the NLRP3 inflammasome (19). Although QS-21 indeed fails to release IL-1β in cells from NLRP3-deficient mice, neither CD8 T cell nor antibody responses to immunization with vaccines containing QS-21 were inhibited in the absence of NLRP3 suggesting that NLRP3 is involved in, but not essential for, the stimulatory effect of QS-21 (17, 18).The combination of MPLA and QS-21 in liposomes to generate AS01 is thought to have synergistic effects by activating multiple signaling pathways in cells and by engaging different cell types (6). Extensive preclinical studies in mice and sheep have emphasized the effect of AS01 on innate immune cells resulting in signals that generate a robust adaptive immune response (20–24). To induce an effective immune response, AS01 and the vaccine antigen need to be injected at the same site, but do not require a physical association, at least for the gE antigen in the shingles vaccine (21). AS01 also does not enhance antigen uptake by antigen-presenting cells. Injection of AS01 in the muscle induced a rapid cytokine response at the injection site and in the draining lymph node (20, 21).Given the differences between the human and mouse immune system (25, 26), including the previously mentioned difference in TLR4 engagement by MPLA, it is important to investigate the MoA of AS01 in humans. Preclinical studies and human clinical data support the concept that AS01 drives a robust IFN-γ response with induction of IFN-γ-related chemokines such as CXCL10 (27), but further insights may be derived from examining the effect of AS01 on human immune cells. Previous studies showed that incubation of human PBMCs with AS01 induced strong expression of TNF and IL-1β in monocytes and, to a lesser extent, dendritic cells (28). However, there was no production of IFN-γ in either T cells or NK cells indicating that further studies are needed to better understand the effect of AS01 in humans.In this study, we investigated the effect of AS01 on the secretion of chemokines, cytokines and growth factors by human immune cells using a large multiplex panel. AS01 induced a robust chemokine response in human monocytic THP-1 cells and PBMCs in addition to the secretion of fewer cytokines and growth factors. Experiments with TLR4-inhibitors and LPs with individual components identified varying contributions of QS-21 and TLR4 agonists to the secretion of chemokines with a remarkable degree of synergy between the two components for the secretion of many chemokines. Our work further revealed a significant induction of IFN-β and IFN-stimulated genes by AS01 which has not been previously reported in preclinical studies. HEK-BlueTM hTLR4 cells (Invivogen, San Diego, CA, USA) were maintained in DMEM supplemented with 2 mM L-glutamine, 100 U/ml penicillin, 100 μg/ml streptomycin, and 100 μg/ml normocin (Invivogen). full_text: AbstractLemierre syndrome is a rare condition characterized by septic thrombophlebitis of the internal jugular vein with metastatic septic emboli, most commonly affecting the lungs. We report a case of Lemierre syndrome temporally associated with influenza A infection in a previously healthy 21-year-old male. The patient initially presented to the emergency department with severe headache and tested positive for influenza A. Over the following seven days, his symptoms progressed to neck pain with decreased range of motion, hemoptysis, cough, and persistent myalgias. Despite four additional emergency department visits, his evolving neck symptoms were attributed to influenza-related myalgias and cervical strain. On the day of admission, examination demonstrated neck swelling, tenderness, restricted jaw opening, and pink foamy sputum. Laboratory studies were significant for severe thrombocytopenia, lactic acidosis, and sepsis. Imaging revealed right mastoid effusion, paranasal sinusitis, multifocal pneumonia, and a near-occlusive thrombus of the right internal jugular vein. Blood cultures grew beta-hemolytic group C Streptococcus and Peptoniphilus asaccharolyticus. The patient was treated with vancomycin, ceftriaxone, clindamycin, and metronidazole. Anticoagulation was initially deferred because of profound thrombocytopenia. Additional therapies included nebulized tranexamic acid, platelet transfusion, corticosteroids, and intravenous immunoglobulin for suspected immune-mediated thrombocytopenia. His hospital course was complicated by metabolic encephalopathy requiring intubation. The patient improved with treatment and was discharged after 17 days on oral antibiotics and rivaroxaban. He was subsequently readmitted 20 days later with a right empyema requiring bronchoscopy, chemical pleurodesis, and decortication. He has remained free of further hospitalization for one year. This case highlights the diagnostic challenges of Lemierre syndrome and the potential for diagnostic anchoring following an initially confirmed viral diagnosis. Although a causal relationship between influenza A infection and Lemierre syndrome cannot be established, clinicians should reassess the diagnosis when patients with confirmed influenza develop persistent or progressive focal symptoms, particularly neck pain or swelling, restricted jaw opening, respiratory symptoms, or systemic deterioration. Early recognition of Lemierre syndrome and prompt treatment are critical to reducing severe complications and morbidity.Keywords: group c streptococcus, influenza a, lemierre syndrome, peptoniphilus asaccharolyticus, septic thrombophlebitis, thrombosis of the internal jugular vein DiscussionThis case of Lemierre syndrome is notable for its development following influenza A infection and for the diagnostic challenges encountered during the patient's clinical course. The patient's presentation ultimately followed the clinical pattern originally described by Dr. Lemierre: a young adult with a preceding head and neck infection who developed bacteremia, septic thrombophlebitis, and subsequent pulmonary complications including empyema [2]. Importantly, the patient's illness initially appeared consistent with influenza A; however, he returned to the emergency department five times over seven days as his symptoms progressively evolved. This case therefore highlights the importance of reassessing an initial diagnosis when a patient's clinical course does not follow the expected trajectory of an uncomplicated viral infection.Prior case reports of Lemierre syndrome following influenza infection have been documented [7,8]; however, influenza is not currently considered a well-established predisposing factor for Lemierre syndrome [7]. One case of Lemierre syndrome following influenza A was reported in the Journal of General and Family Medicine in 2019. In that case, a 24-year-old woman developed multiple cavitary lung lesions and left internal jugular vein thrombosis one week after being diagnosed with influenza A and treated with oseltamivir; blood cultures grew Fusobacterium [7]. Another case reported in 2011 described a four-year-old child who, following positive influenza A testing and beta-hemolytic streptococcal pharyngitis, developed septic thrombophlebitis of the left jugular vein, although blood cultures remained negative [8].Influenza may increase susceptibility to secondary bacterial infections through mechanisms including mucosal injury, transient immune dysfunction, and disruption of the normal epithelial barrier. In our patient, influenza A was detected during the initial emergency department presentation, and CT imaging demonstrated acute sinusitis two days later. This temporal relationship between influenza A infection, subsequent sinusitis, and eventual development of Lemierre syndrome raises the possibility that influenza-associated mucosal inflammation or immune dysfunction contributed to secondary bacterial infection in this case. However, a causal relationship cannot be established from a single case. Rather than demonstrating that influenza predisposes patients to Lemierre syndrome, this case adds to the limited number of reported cases describing this temporal association.A more important clinical lesson from this case is the potential for diagnostic anchoring when a common viral diagnosis provides an initial explanation for nonspecific symptoms. Influenza can reasonably account for symptoms such as headache, myalgias, cough, and malaise; however, our patient's subsequent development of focal neck pain, restricted jaw opening, neck swelling, and hemoptysis represented a significant change from an uncomplicated influenza presentation. His repeated emergency department visits over seven days further demonstrate the importance of reassessing the initial diagnostic impression when symptoms persist, worsen, or evolve in an unexpected manner. In patients with a recent respiratory or head and neck infection, progressive unilateral neck symptoms, trismus, respiratory symptoms, or systemic toxicity should prompt consideration of a deeper bacterial infection and potential septic thrombophlebitis. Early recognition may allow for earlier imaging, antimicrobial therapy, and appropriate multidisciplinary management.The development of an empyema following treatment for Lemierre syndrome is also consistent with the pulmonary complications associated with this disease. Dr. Lemierre described secondary localization to the lungs as a characteristic manifestation of the syndrome [2]. Pulmonary complications, most commonly related to septic pulmonary emboli, are reported frequently in Lemierre syndrome [1]. In our patient, multifocal pneumonia was identified during the initial hospitalization, followed by development of a right-sided empyema requiring bronchoscopy, chemical pleurodesis, and decortication. This progression illustrates the potential for continued metastatic infection despite initial treatment and emphasizes the importance of close clinical follow-up.Fusobacterium necrophorum is the organism most commonly associated with Lemierre syndrome, although its presence is not required for diagnosis [9,10]. Our patient's blood cultures instead grew beta-hemolytic group C Streptococcus and Peptoniphilus asaccharolyticus. Streptococcal species have been described as causative organisms in Lemierre syndrome [1,3,9] and were also noted in Dr. Lemierre's original description [2]. Although less common than Fusobacterium, these findings demonstrate that Lemierre syndrome should remain a consideration even when blood cultures do not identify the classically associated organism. Peptoniphilus asaccharolyticus is an anaerobic organism and, to our knowledge, has not previously been reported as a causative organism of Lemierre syndrome. full_text_sections.abstract: AbstractLemierre syndrome is a rare condition characterized by septic thrombophlebitis of the internal jugular vein with metastatic septic emboli, most commonly affecting the lungs. We report a case of Lemierre syndrome temporally associated with influenza A infection in a previously healthy 21-year-old male. The patient initially presented to the emergency department with severe headache and tested positive for influenza A. Over the following seven days, his symptoms progressed to neck pain with decreased range of motion, hemoptysis, cough, and persistent myalgias. Despite four additional emergency department visits, his evolving neck symptoms were attributed to influenza-related myalgias and cervical strain. On the day of admission, examination demonstrated neck swelling, tenderness, restricted jaw opening, and pink foamy sputum. Laboratory studies were significant for severe thrombocytopenia, lactic acidosis, and sepsis. Imaging revealed right mastoid effusion, paranasal sinusitis, multifocal pneumonia, and a near-occlusive thrombus of the right internal jugular vein. Blood cultures grew beta-hemolytic group C Streptococcus and Peptoniphilus asaccharolyticus. The patient was treated with vancomycin, ceftriaxone, clindamycin, and metronidazole. Anticoagulation was initially deferred because of profound thrombocytopenia. Additional therapies included nebulized tranexamic acid, platelet transfusion, corticosteroids, and intravenous immunoglobulin for suspected immune-mediated thrombocytopenia. His hospital course was complicated by metabolic encephalopathy requiring intubation. The patient improved with treatment and was discharged after 17 days on oral antibiotics and rivaroxaban. He was subsequently readmitted 20 days later with a right empyema requiring bronchoscopy, chemical pleurodesis, and decortication. He has remained free of further hospitalization for one year. This case highlights the diagnostic challenges of Lemierre syndrome and the potential for diagnostic anchoring following an initially confirmed viral diagnosis. Although a causal relationship between influenza A infection and Lemierre syndrome cannot be established, clinicians should reassess the diagnosis when patients with confirmed influenza develop persistent or progressive focal symptoms, particularly neck pain or swelling, restricted jaw opening, respiratory symptoms, or systemic deterioration. Early recognition of Lemierre syndrome and prompt treatment are critical to reducing severe complications and morbidity.Keywords: group c streptococcus, influenza a, lemierre syndrome, peptoniphilus asaccharolyticus, septic thrombophlebitis, thrombosis of the internal jugular vein
full_text_sections.discussion: DiscussionThis case of Lemierre syndrome is notable for its development following influenza A infection and for the diagnostic challenges encountered during the patient's clinical course. The patient's presentation ultimately followed the clinical pattern originally described by Dr. Lemierre: a young adult with a preceding head and neck infection who developed bacteremia, septic thrombophlebitis, and subsequent pulmonary complications including empyema [2]. Importantly, the patient's illness initially appeared consistent with influenza A; however, he returned to the emergency department five times over seven days as his symptoms progressively evolved. This case therefore highlights the importance of reassessing an initial diagnosis when a patient's clinical course does not follow the expected trajectory of an uncomplicated viral infection.Prior case reports of Lemierre syndrome following influenza infection have been documented [7,8]; however, influenza is not currently considered a well-established predisposing factor for Lemierre syndrome [7]. One case of Lemierre syndrome following influenza A was reported in the Journal of General and Family Medicine in 2019. In that case, a 24-year-old woman developed multiple cavitary lung lesions and left internal jugular vein thrombosis one week after being diagnosed with influenza A and treated with oseltamivir; blood cultures grew Fusobacterium [7]. Another case reported in 2011 described a four-year-old child who, following positive influenza A testing and beta-hemolytic streptococcal pharyngitis, developed septic thrombophlebitis of the left jugular vein, although blood cultures remained negative [8].Influenza may increase susceptibility to secondary bacterial infections through mechanisms including mucosal injury, transient immune dysfunction, and disruption of the normal epithelial barrier. In our patient, influenza A was detected during the initial emergency department presentation, and CT imaging demonstrated acute sinusitis two days later. This temporal relationship between influenza A infection, subsequent sinusitis, and eventual development of Lemierre syndrome raises the possibility that influenza-associated mucosal inflammation or immune dysfunction contributed to secondary bacterial infection in this case. However, a causal relationship cannot be established from a single case. Rather than demonstrating that influenza predisposes patients to Lemierre syndrome, this case adds to the limited number of reported cases describing this temporal association.A more important clinical lesson from this case is the potential for diagnostic anchoring when a common viral diagnosis provides an initial explanation for nonspecific symptoms. Influenza can reasonably account for symptoms such as headache, myalgias, cough, and malaise; however, our patient's subsequent development of focal neck pain, restricted jaw opening, neck swelling, and hemoptysis represented a significant change from an uncomplicated influenza presentation. His repeated emergency department visits over seven days further demonstrate the importance of reassessing the initial diagnostic impression when symptoms persist, worsen, or evolve in an unexpected manner. In patients with a recent respiratory or head and neck infection, progressive unilateral neck symptoms, trismus, respiratory symptoms, or systemic toxicity should prompt consideration of a deeper bacterial infection and potential septic thrombophlebitis. Early recognition may allow for earlier imaging, antimicrobial therapy, and appropriate multidisciplinary management.The development of an empyema following treatment for Lemierre syndrome is also consistent with the pulmonary complications associated with this disease. Dr. Lemierre described secondary localization to the lungs as a characteristic manifestation of the syndrome [2]. Pulmonary complications, most commonly related to septic pulmonary emboli, are reported frequently in Lemierre syndrome [1]. In our patient, multifocal pneumonia was identified during the initial hospitalization, followed by development of a right-sided empyema requiring bronchoscopy, chemical pleurodesis, and decortication. This progression illustrates the potential for continued metastatic infection despite initial treatment and emphasizes the importance of close clinical follow-up.Fusobacterium necrophorum is the organism most commonly associated with Lemierre syndrome, although its presence is not required for diagnosis [9,10]. Our patient's blood cultures instead grew beta-hemolytic group C Streptococcus and Peptoniphilus asaccharolyticus. Streptococcal species have been described as causative organisms in Lemierre syndrome [1,3,9] and were also noted in Dr. Lemierre's original description [2]. Peptoniphilus asaccharolyticus is an anaerobic organism and, to our knowledge, has not previously been reported as a causative organism of Lemierre syndrome. The polymicrobial nature of the bacteremia in this case further supports maintaining a broad microbiologic differential when evaluating suspected Lemierre syndrome.At this time, it remains unclear whether influenza A infection directly predisposed this patient to the development of Lemierre syndrome. The temporal association between influenza A infection, subsequent sinusitis, and the development of septic internal jugular vein thrombophlebitis with pulmonary complications is notable, but causality cannot be established. The primary clinical lesson from this case is the importance of diagnostic reassessment when a patient's symptoms persist or evolve beyond the expected course of an initial diagnosis. In patients with recent influenza or other respiratory infections who develop progressive neck pain or swelling, restricted jaw opening, hemoptysis, respiratory symptoms, or systemic deterioration, clinicians should maintain a broad differential diagnosis and consider secondary bacterial infection and Lemierre syndrome. Early recognition of this rare but potentially life-threatening condition may reduce the risk of severe complications from septic thrombophlebitis and metastatic infection.

full_text: Abstract Unlike that of T2 asthma, the pathophysiology of non–T2 asthma remains largely unexplored. However, increasing evidence supports a role for trained macrophages in asthma. In this study, we utilized a non-T2 asthma mouse model associated with early respiratory viral infection to identify the H3K27me3-NR1D1-IFN-γ axis in lung-trained macrophages, which drives non-T2 asthma by promoting Th1 differentiation. Early infection combined with allergen sensitization induced the formation of trained macrophages, which displayed hyperactive methionine cycling and elevated levels of S-adenosylmethionine (SAM). As a substrate for methyltransferase, SAM enhanced the trimethylation of H3K27, subsequently suppressing the expression of the nuclear receptor subfamily 1 group D member 1 (NR1D1) gene through enrichment at its promoter. Interestingly, NR1D1 interacted with the Ifng gene and negatively regulated its expression. High levels of IFN-γ from trained macrophages were observed because NR1D1 was inhibited by elevated H3K27me3 levels. Following allergen challenge, the increased expression of IFN-γ, MHC-II, and CD80/CD86 in trained macrophages positively regulated the activation and differentiation of Th1 cells, which subsequently produced more IFN-γ, thereby promoting non-T2 asthma. Consistently, in patients with asthma, peripheral blood mononuclear cells (PBMCs) and monocytes downregulated NR1D1 expression, resulting in elevated IFN-γ levels. Conversely, treatment of patient monocytes with an NR1D1 agonist led to a marked decrease in IFN-γ production. In mice, non-T2 asthma was significantly inhibited by either the inhibition of H3K27me3, the activation of NR1D1, or the neutralization of IFN-γ. Our results demonstrate that the H3K27me3-NR1D1-IFN-γ axis in lung-trained macrophages, which is associated with early infection, drives non-T2 asthma during childhood in mice. Consequently, SAM, NR1D1, and IFN-γ may serve as potential drug targets for the treatment of non-T2 asthma. full_text_sections.full_text: Abstract Unlike that of T2 asthma, the pathophysiology of non–T2 asthma remains largely unexplored. However, increasing evidence supports a role for trained macrophages in asthma. In this study, we utilized a non-T2 asthma mouse model associated with early respiratory viral infection to identify the H3K27me3-NR1D1-IFN-γ axis in lung-trained macrophages, which drives non-T2 asthma by promoting Th1 differentiation. Early infection combined with allergen sensitization induced the formation of trained macrophages, which displayed hyperactive methionine cycling and elevated levels of S-adenosylmethionine (SAM). As a substrate for methyltransferase, SAM enhanced the trimethylation of H3K27, subsequently suppressing the expression of the nuclear receptor subfamily 1 group D member 1 (NR1D1) gene through enrichment at its promoter. Interestingly, NR1D1 interacted with the Ifng gene and negatively regulated its expression. High levels of IFN-γ from trained macrophages were observed because NR1D1 was inhibited by elevated H3K27me3 levels. Following allergen challenge, the increased expression of IFN-γ, MHC-II, and CD80/CD86 in trained macrophages positively regulated the activation and differentiation of Th1 cells, which subsequently produced more IFN-γ, thereby promoting non-T2 asthma. Consistently, in patients with asthma, peripheral blood mononuclear cells (PBMCs) and monocytes downregulated NR1D1 expression, resulting in elevated IFN-γ levels. Conversely, treatment of patient monocytes with an NR1D1 agonist led to a marked decrease in IFN-γ production. In mice, non-T2 asthma was significantly inhibited by either the inhibition of H3K27me3, the activation of NR1D1, or the neutralization of IFN-γ. Our results demonstrate that the H3K27me3-NR1D1-IFN-γ axis in lung-trained macrophages, which is associated with early infection, drives non-T2 asthma during childhood in mice. Consequently, SAM, NR1D1, and IFN-γ may serve as potential drug targets for the treatment of non-T2 asthma. title_original: The H3K27me3-NR1D1-IFN-γ axis in trained macrophages induced by early respiratory virus infection drives non-T2 asthma in children

analysis.research_question_and_background: The study aimed to investigate the pathophysiology of non-T2 asthma, which remains largely unexplored, and to identify mechanisms by which early respiratory viral infection contributes to its development.
analysis.study_design_and_population: The study used a non-T2 asthma mouse model induced by early respiratory viral infection combined with allergen sensitization. The model involved trained macrophages that displayed hyperactive methionine cycling and elevated levels of S-adenosylmethionine (SAM).
analysis.methods: The methods included the use of a non-T2 asthma mouse model, allergen challenge, and analysis of gene expression and cytokine levels in trained macrophages. SAM levels were linked to H3K27me3 trimethylation, which was shown to suppress NR1D1 gene expression through promoter enrichment.
analysis.main_results: Following allergen challenge, trained macrophages showed increased expression of IFN-γ, MHC-II, and CD80/CD86, which positively regulated Th1 cell activation and differentiation. In patients with asthma, PBMCs and monocytes downregulated NR1D1 expression, resulting in elevated IFN-γ levels.
analysis.interpretation_and_novelty: The authors interpreted that the H3K27me3-NR1D1-IFN-γ axis in lung-trained macrophages, associated with early infection, drives non-T2 asthma in children, offering a novel mechanistic insight into the development of this asthma subtype.
analysis.scientific_and_public_health_significanc: The findings suggest that targeting SAM, NR1D1, or IFN-γ could provide therapeutic options for non-T2 asthma, potentially informing future research and treatment strategies for this condition.
analysis.limitations_and_evidence_strength: The study is limited by its reliance on a mouse model and the lack of direct human clinical trials. However, the results are supported by consistent findings in both mice and human asthma patients, providing moderate confidence in the proposed mechanism.

analysis.summary_en: This study explores the pathophysiology of non-T2 asthma, which is less understood compared to T2 asthma. The research focuses on the role of early respiratory viral infection in inducing trained macrophages, which contribute to non-T2 asthma through the H3K27me3-NR1D1-IFN-γ axis. The study demonstrates that SAM enhances H3K27me3 trimethylation, suppressing NR1D1 expression and leading to elevated IFN-γ levels. These findings suggest that the H3K27me3-NR1D1-IFN-γ pathway may be a potential therapeutic target for non-T2 asthma. The results are supported by both in vivo and in vitro evidence, though the study is limited to a mouse model and lacks direct human clinical trials. The implications of the study highlight the importance of understanding the interplay between viral infections and immune responses in childhood asthma.

source_body_en: In this study, we utilized a non-T2 asthma mouse model associated with early respiratory viral infection to identify the H3K27me3-NR1D1-IFN-γ axis in lung-trained macrophages, which drives non-T2 asthma by promoting Th1 differentiation. Our results demonstrate that the H3K27me3-NR1D1-IFN-γ axis in lung-trained macrophages, which is associated with early infection, drives non-T2 asthma during childhood in mice. A review of epigenetic changes in asthma: methylation and acetylation. Abstract Unlike that of T2 asthma, the pathophysiology of non–T2 asthma remains largely unexplored. However, increasing evidence supports a role for trained macrophages in asthma. Early infection combined with allergen sensitization induced the formation of trained macrophages, which displayed hyperactive methionine cycling and elevated levels of S-adenosylmethionine (SAM). As a substrate for methyltransferase, SAM enhanced the trimethylation of H3K27, subsequently suppressing the expression of the nuclear receptor subfamily 1 group D member 1 (NR1D1) gene through enrichment at its promoter. Interestingly, NR1D1 interacted with the Ifng gene and negatively regulated its expression. High levels of IFN-γ from trained macrophages were observed because NR1D1 was inhibited by elevated H3K27me3 levels. Following allergen challenge, the increased expression of IFN-γ, MHC-II, and CD80/CD86 in trained macrophages positively regulated the activation and differentiation of Th1 cells, which subsequently produced more IFN-γ, thereby promoting non-T2 asthma. Consistently, in patients with asthma, peripheral blood mononuclear cells (PBMCs) and monocytes downregulated NR1D1 expression, resulting in elevated IFN-γ levels.
